Complete Entanglement Structure of the Kitaev Honeycomb Spin Liquid from Exact Tensor Networks

Hidehiro Saito Email: saito-hidehiro722@g.ecc.u-tokyo.ac.jp Affiliation: Department of Basic Science, University of Tokyo, Meguro-ku, Tokyo 153-8902, Japan    Chisa Hotta Email: chisa@phys.c.u-tokyo.ac.jp Affiliation: Department of Basic Science, University of Tokyo, Meguro-ku, Tokyo 153-8902, Japan
October 4, 2026
Abstract

While most of the features of the Kitaev honeycomb model are already clarified from the combined ℤ2{\mathbb{Z}}_{2} plaquette and Majorana fermion picture, we show that retrieving the exact quantum many-body form gives a clue to fix the remaining issues on its spin liquid property. We provide an exact two-dimensional tensor network description of a full set of solutions from a random product state, by sequential quantum-number projection and Gutzwiller projection, both expressed as local matrix-product operators of dimension D=2D=2. The ground and excited states share the same bond dimension yet exhibit distinct Schmidt spectra, distinguishing their area-law and volume-law entanglement. We demonstrate that the topological entanglement entropy emerges for all eigenstates only after the Gutzwiller projection onto the physical spin Hilbert space, where the gauge constraint removes exactly half of the Schmidt states. This establishes that excited states are likewise topologically ordered. We further show that there exists a projection-induced collapse of the wave function into a single gauge sector in the Parton mean-field states that is known to give a good description of the spin liquids. The demonstrations on the S=1/2S=1/2 kagome and triangular Heisenberg models suggest that the present perspective is applied to a wider class of models hosting ℤ2{\mathbb{Z}}_{2} spin liquids. Our finding visualizes a bulk-boundary correspondence with the Wilson-loop characterization of topological order.

I Introduction

The Kitaev honeycomb model [1] has long served as a canonical platform for realizing a ℤ2{\mathbb{Z}}_{2} quantum spin liquid (QSL), owing to its analytical tractability using classical ℤ2{\mathbb{Z}}_{2} plaquettes and free Majorana fermions. In candidate materials like Li2IrO3, Na2IrO3[2, 3, 4] and α\alpha-RuCl2[5, 6], additional Heisenberg or Γ\Gamma interactions are present that make the state no longer exactly solvable[7, 8, 9]. Still, the insights from the Kitaev limit help their understanding, with Majorana fermions regarded as a hallmark of the QSL[10].

However, the true QSL wavefunction is not the bare Majorana state but its Gutzwiller projection onto the physical Hilbert space. Since this distinction does not explicitly affect most of the non-topological thermodynamic properties[11], it was not clear whether the post-projected states that are no longer treated analytically, can have more importance. Mathematically, for fermionic models with four Majorana modes, one can construct a solvable toric-code type Hamiltonian[12] that commutes with the loop-forming Gutzwiller projector, and this projection is indispensable to have the topological order of that Hamiltonian[13]. For generic models, however, the projection cannot be carried out analytically, making an explicit quantum many-body formulation of the QSL essential to address this issue.

Unfortunately, only a few works have constructed exact quantum many-body states of the Kitaev honeycomb model. Tensor-network (TN) representation of the ground state was successfully obtained by encoding the Jordan-Wigner, Fourier, and Bogoliubov transformations into a 3D unitary TN circuit of polynomial depth[14]. However, the fermionic operation in such standard TN generally requires a relatively complex algorithm. 11 1 In Ref.[14], decomposing the operations including Jordan-Wigner, Fourier, and Bogoliubov transformations to 2-qubit gates require explicit fermionic SWAP gates, which are extra to the standard TN for the spin Hamiltonian. Our method also treats fermions, but the fermionic swaps are implicitly encoded in the single-site MPO, and requires no extra treatment compared to the projection operation developed in Ref.[57] to obtain an exact solution for the frustration-free spin Hamiltonian. The computational cost of Ref.[14] is measured by the polynomial depth unitary circuit, which is comparable to our O⁡(N)O(N) cost. The memory cost should also be comparable if one performs the same size calculation without approximation Approximate two-dimensional TN states based on projected entangled pair states (PEPS) have also been proposed [16]; they break the QSL symmetry while restoring it variationally to some extent, and are largely restricted to the ground state[17]. The approximation sacrifices the accurate description of the underlying gauge structure, e.g., mixes different topological sectors, and raises difficulty in the evaluation of the entanglement spectrum. Some works on infinite cylinders have succeeded in separating the topological sectors and the entanglement spectrum for the approximate DMRG states[18, 19]. However, obtaining the numerically exact entanglement spectrum for a sufficiently large system remains an utmost challenge.

In this paper, we propose an exact and simple two-dimensional TN representation of the full spectrum of the Kitaev honeycomb model. The construction relies on matrix-product-operator (MPO) representations[20, 21, 22] of the global projectors associated with plaquette and Majorana fermion quantum numbers, reducible to products of local MPOs with bond dimension D=2D=2 and no additional fermionic SWAP gates. Starting from a randomized one-dimensional matrix product state (MPS)[23, 21], we successively apply these projectors while truncating idle bonds, and finally perform a Gutzwiller projection from Majorana to spin degrees of freedom. Our TN enables efficient local operations, including Majorana braiding, bipartition, and spatially local projections, via product-MPO manipulations. We find that the topological entanglement entropy(EE) [24, 25], −ln⁡2-\ln 2, appears only after the Gutzwiller projection. The projection reduces all the Schmidt states exactly by half, as they allow only one of the two mutually exclusive ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}-gauge states to survive. Similar collapse of the Schmidt states by the Gutzwiller projection also occurs in the spin-liquid state of the S=1/2S=1/2 kagome antiferromagnet, despite the absence of explicit gauge variables or loop degrees of freedom in its Hamiltonian. The underlying global gauge constraint on the Hilbert space is therefore an intrinsic property of emergent topological order, providing a visible bulk counterpart to the boundary gauge sector characterized by Wilson loops [26, 27].

II Formulation

II.1 Preliminaries

We consider a spin-1/2 Kitaev honeycomb model on a N=2​Nx×NyN=2N_{x}\times N_{y} lattice (Fig. 1(a)) with a periodic boundary condition(PBC) given as

ℋ=−∑⟨j​k⟩γJγσ^γjσ^γk,{\cal H}=-\sum_{\langle jk\rangle^{\gamma}}J_{\gamma}\hat{\sigma}^{\gamma}_{j}\hat{\sigma}^{\gamma}_{k}, (1)

where ⟨j​k⟩γ\langle jk\rangle^{\gamma} runs over all nearest neighbor sites, and γ=x,y,z\gamma=x,y,z denotes either of the three different directions the j​kjk-bond is pointing. The up/down spin degrees of freedom are extended to the representation of four Majorana fermions, b^ix,b^iy,b^iz,c^i\hat{b}_{i}^{x},\hat{b}_{i}^{y},\hat{b}_{i}^{z},\hat{c}_{i}, where σ^iα=i​b^iα​c^i\hat{\sigma}_{i}^{\alpha}=i\hat{b}^{\alpha}_{i}\hat{c}_{i}. For the ⟨j​k⟩γ\langle jk\rangle^{\gamma} neighbors, these Majoranas form a bond operator given as, u^j​k=i​b^jγ​b^kγ\hat{u}_{jk}=i\hat{b}_{j}^{\gamma}\hat{b}_{k}^{\gamma}, and by using them, Eq.(1) is rewritten in the quadratic form,

ℋM=i​∑⟨j​k⟩γJγ​u^j​k​c^j​c^k.{\cal H}_{M}=i\sum_{\langle jk\rangle^{\gamma}}J_{\gamma}\hat{u}_{jk}\hat{c}_{j}\hat{c}_{k}. (2)

Here, because [ℋM,u^j​k]=0[{\cal H}_{M},\hat{u}_{jk}]=0, and u^j​k\hat{u}_{jk} has the eigenvalue uj​k=±1u_{jk}=\pm 1, this Majorana Hamiltonian is block diagonalized into the subspace specified by a set of quantum numbers 𝒖={uj​k}\bm{u}=\{u_{jk}\} over 23​N/22^{3N/2} different combinations. Suppose we have one such set, and the resultant matrix representation of the Hamiltonian on that subspace is given in the N×NN\times N form, i​A={2​i​Jγ​uj​k}j,k=1NiA=\{2iJ_{\gamma}u_{jk}\}_{j,k=1}^{N}, with its elements satisfying uj​k=−uk​ju_{jk}=-u_{kj}. Diagonalizing it as i​A=Q​E​Q†iA=QEQ^{\dagger}, we find, ℋM=∑ℓ=1N/2ϵℓ​(a^ℓ†​a^ℓ−1/2){\cal H}_{M}=\sum_{\ell=1}^{N/2}\epsilon_{\ell}(\hat{a}_{\ell}^{\dagger}\hat{a}_{\ell}-1/2), where a^ℓ=1/2∑j=1NQj​ℓc^j\hat{a}_{\ell}=1/\sqrt{2}\sum_{j=1}^{N}Q_{j\ell}\hat{c}_{j} satisfies a^ℓ=a^N+1−ℓ†\hat{a}_{\ell}=\hat{a}_{N+1-\ell}^{\dagger} when diag​E={−ϵℓ}l=1N{\rm diag}E=\{-\epsilon_{\ell}\}_{l=1}^{N} is arranged in ascending order.

The Majorana fermion number operator is, n^ℓ=a^ℓ†​a^ℓ\hat{n}_{\ell}=\hat{a}_{\ell}^{\dagger}\hat{a}_{\ell}, where nℓ=0n_{\ell}=0 or 1. Therefore, each eigenstate |Ψ~𝒖,𝒏M⟩|\tilde{\Psi}_{\bm{u},\bm{n}}^{M}\rangle of ℋM{\cal H}_{M} has the quantum numbers, 𝒖={uj​k}\bm{u}=\{u_{jk}\} and 𝒏={nℓ}\bm{n}=\{n_{\ell}\}. To put these eigenstates back to those of the physical Hamiltonian, the operator, D^i=b^ix​b^iy​b^iz​c^i\hat{D}_{i}=\hat{b}_{i}^{x}\hat{b}_{i}^{y}\hat{b}_{i}^{z}\hat{c}_{i}, whose eigenvalue is ±1\pm 1, is useful, as the sector Di=1D_{i}=1 forms a subspace of spin degrees of freedom on site ii. Using their products, the fermionic wave function is projected onto the original Hilbert space as

|Ψ𝒖,𝒏⟩∝𝒫D​|Ψ~𝒖,𝒏M⟩,𝒫D=∏i=1N1+D^i2.|\Psi_{\bm{u},\bm{n}}\rangle\propto{\cal P}_{D}|\tilde{\Psi}_{\bm{u},\bm{n}}^{M}\rangle,\quad{\cal P}_{D}=\prod_{i=1}^{N}\frac{1+\hat{D}_{i}}{2}. (3)

These preliminary formulas are well established [1].

II.2 Exact tensor network

For a given values of quantum numbers, 𝒖={uj​k}=±1\bm{u}=\{u_{jk}\}=\pm 1 and 𝒏={nℓ}=\bm{n}=\{n_{\ell}\}= 0 or 1, there are corresponding projectors given in the form,

𝒫u\displaystyle{\cal P}_{u} =∏⟨j​k⟩γp^j​k,p^j​k=1±u^j​k2,(j<k,uj​k=±1)\displaystyle=\prod_{\langle jk\rangle^{\gamma}}\hat{p}_{jk},\quad\hat{p}_{jk}=\frac{1\pm\hat{u}_{jk}}{2},\;(j<k,\;u_{jk}=\pm 1) (4)
𝒫a\displaystyle{\cal P}_{a} =∏ℓ=1N/2q^ℓ,q^ℓ={a^ℓ†​a^ℓ(nℓ=1)a^ℓ​a^ℓ†(nℓ=0),\displaystyle=\prod_{\ell=1}^{N/2}\hat{q}_{\ell},\quad\quad\hat{q}_{\ell}=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\hat{a}_{\ell}^{\dagger}\hat{a}_{\ell}&(n_{\ell}=1)\\ \hat{a}_{\ell}\hat{a}_{\ell}^{\dagger}&(n_{\ell}=0)\end{array}\right.,

where for j>kj>k, p^j​k=(1∓u^k​j)/2\hat{p}_{jk}=(1\mp\hat{u}_{kj})/2. Previously, fermionic MPS-MPO representations with a graphical structure similar to Fig. 1(b) were developed as variational ansatz for ground states [28, 29, 30]. Our framework differs conceptually: rather than constructing the target state by applying fermionic creation operators to the vacuum[31], we start from a maximally informative random state and extract the target Hilbert subspace by projection. This philosophical difference is analogous to the contrast between METTS [32] and TPQ [33] for thermal states, where the former builds a mixed state as an ensemble of initially unentangled product states by minimally developing entanglement, whereas the latter projects a highly entangled random state into a single pure state.

Exact eigenstates are obtained because the projectors p^j​k\hat{p}_{jk} and q^ℓ\hat{q}_{\ell} admit a factorized MPO representation, with each local tensor acting only on a single-site Hilbert space. We construct such a representation using MPOs acting on an MPS wavefunction defined on a finite cluster with PBC. The MPS is defined along a helical path covering the two-dimensional lattice, as illustrated in Fig. 1(a). For the single-site fermionic basis of dimension d=4d=4 defined as |0⟩,|↑⟩,|↓⟩,|↑↓⟩|0\rangle,|\uparrow\rangle,|\downarrow\rangle,|\uparrow\downarrow\rangle [34, 35], the MPO of p^j​k\hat{p}_{jk} and q^ℓ\hat{q}_{\ell} acting on the γ\gamma-th bond and ℓ\ell-th site can be represented with bond dimension D=2D=2 as

where F↑=diag​(1,−1,1,−1)F_{\uparrow}=\textrm{diag}(1,-1,1,-1), F↓=diag​(1,1,−1,−1)F_{\downarrow}=\textrm{diag}(1,1,-1,-1), and Fj=F↑​F↓F_{j}=F_{\uparrow}F_{\downarrow} is the fermion string required by the anticommutation relation, F~j(i)=Fj\tilde{F}_{j}^{\rm(i)}=F_{j} (γ=x,y\gamma=x,y) and F↓F_{\downarrow} (γ=z\gamma=z), and F~k(f)=Ik\tilde{F}_{k}^{\rm(f)}=I_{k} (γ=x,y\gamma=x,y) and F↑F_{\uparrow} (γ=z\gamma=z).

In addition to the local MPO, the key to obtaining a numerically exact MPS eigenstate is to start from an initial random product state |Ψ~random⟩|\tilde{\Psi}_{\rm random}\rangle, where χ=1\chi=1 turns out sufficient. By operating Eqs.(4) and (II.2), we obtain the exact TN eigenstate as

|Ψ~𝒖,𝒏M⟩=𝒫a​𝒫u​|Ψ~random⟩,|\tilde{\Psi}^{M}_{\bm{u},\bm{n}}\rangle={\cal P}_{a}{\cal P}_{u}|\tilde{\Psi}_{\rm random}\rangle, (9)

which is graphically illustrated in Fig. 1(b). At each step of applying p^j​k\hat{p}_{jk} or q^ℓ\hat{q}_{\ell}, we Schmidt decompose the state and discard the idle bond dimension. The local contraction is allowed because Eq.(7) is a product of local operators. This process does not imply an approximation 22 2 The numerical accuracy of the ground state and randomly chosen excited state at N=32N=32 when starting from the bond dimension D=1D=1 are |⟨ℋ⟩−Eexact|=2.85×10−10|\langle{\cal H}\rangle-E_{\rm exact}|=2.85\times 10^{-10} and 2.66×10−152.66\times 10^{-15}, respectively, against the analytical exact solutions EexactE_{\rm exact}., unlike the standard variational usage of MPS that uses finite χ\chi by discarding small Schmidt states. Finally, on the last row of the figure, the Gutzwiller single-site MPO, Eq.(3), is applied to make it the eigenstate of Eq.(1).

Before performing these processes, we need to choose 𝒖\bm{u} and 𝒏\bm{n} to satisfy the conservation laws; There are N/2+2N/2+2 loop operators commuting with the Hamiltonian: two global loop operators, Wx,WyW_{x},W_{y}, winding around torus, and N/2N/2 plaquette operators W^p=∏j∈ℒpσjαj\hat{W}_{p}=\prod_{j\in{\cal L}_{p}}\sigma_{j}^{\alpha_{j}}, where αj=x,y,z\alpha_{j}=x,y,z denotes the bond connected to site jj but not included in the loop. Considering the constraint, ∏p=1N/2W^p=1^\prod_{p=1}^{N/2}\hat{W}_{p}=\hat{1}, there are N/2+1N/2+1 independent conserved ℤ​2\mathbb{Z}2 quantum numbers, wp,wx,wy{w_{p},w_{x},w_{y}}, which determine 𝒖\bm{u}. Furthermore, 𝒖\bm{u} and 𝒏\bm{n} must satisfy the projection constraint D^=∏i=1ND^i=1^\hat{D}=\prod_{i=1}^{N}\hat{D}_{i}=\hat{1}[37, 25, 38, 39]. Details are provided in Appendix A.

III Numerical representativity

We numerically perform the above calculation on the N=2​Nx×Ny=32N=2N_{x}\times N_{y}=32 site cluster, and test the representativity of our TN.

III.1 Braiding

The prominent advantage of our TN is to easily obtain and manipulate any of the excited states. The braiding operation is local and simple (Fig. 1(c)). Let the initial state |Ψ(i)​[α,β]⟩|\Psi^{(i)}[\alpha,\beta]\rangle has {wp,wx,wy}={1,1,1}\{w_{p},w_{x},w_{y}\}=\{1,1,1\}, except for two colored hexagons, wα=wβ=−1w_{\alpha}=w_{\beta}=-1. We now move the flux on α\alpha around β\beta, which is done by operating σiγ\sigma_{i}^{\gamma} with γ\gamma the bond label that the moving plaquette crosses. As it is a single-site operation to our TN on six different sites, the final state, |Ψ(f)​[α,β]⟩=σ6y​σ5z​σ4x​σ3y​σ2z​σ1x​|Ψ(i)​[α,β]⟩|\Psi^{(f)}[\alpha,\beta]\rangle=\sigma_{6}^{y}\sigma_{5}^{z}\sigma_{4}^{x}\sigma_{3}^{y}\sigma_{2}^{z}\sigma_{1}^{x}|\Psi^{(i)}[\alpha,\beta]\rangle, is immediately obtained and shows ⟨Ψ(i)​[α,β]|Ψ(f)​[α,β]⟩=Wβ=−1\langle\Psi^{(i)}[\alpha,\beta]|\Psi^{(f)}[\alpha,\beta]\rangle=W_{\beta}=-1.

III.2 Entanglement entropy

Figure 2(a) shows the entanglement entropy (EE), SS, about the bipartition mm to N−mN-m (see Fig. 1(a)) for the ground state and the excited state, where for the latter, we take the randomly chosen sector, 𝒖,𝒏\bm{u},\bm{n}. The excited state shows a typical volume law behavior (Appendix A.3), and the ground state exhibits an area-law plateau. We test in Fig. 2(b) the size scaling of SN/2S_{N/2} for both the fermionic |Ψ~u,nM⟩|\tilde{\Psi}^{M}_{u,n}\rangle and physical state |Ψu,n⟩|{\Psi}_{u,n}\rangle. Both cases are exactly linear-in-NyN_{y} with equal slopes for different choices of Nx=2,3,4N_{x}=2,3,4. Notably, the physical ground state has a finite topological term, −ln⁡2-\ln 2, that identifies the ℤ2{\mathbb{Z}}_{2} QSL, whereas the intercept is zero for a fermionic eigenstate. The same reduction of EE by −ln⁡2-\ln 2 after projection appears for the excited states. Interestingly, we find that when 𝒫D{\cal P}_{D} is applied to |Ψ~u,nM⟩|\tilde{\Psi}^{M}_{u,n}\rangle, the number of Schmidt states at the bipartition is exactly reduced by half for each Schmidt value and the value λq\lambda_{q} is scaled by 2\sqrt{2} instead (Fig. 2(d)). This means that the whole solution space is reduced simultaneously by half, and this applies to all eigenstates.

As all the solutions are exact, the number of nonzero Schmidt values is equal to the bond dimension χm\chi_{m}. Figure 2(c) shows χm\chi_{m} as functions of mm, where we find that they are exactly the same for all eigenstates. The maximum value at the system center, is given as χmax=2(Nx+2)​Ny/2,2(Nx+2)​Ny/2−1\chi_{\rm max}=2^{(N_{x}+2)N_{y}/2},2^{(N_{x}+2)N_{y}/2-1}, respectively, for the fermionic and physical states. In general, χmax\chi_{\rm max} grows in power and exponential of system size for the states with area law and volume law EE, respectively. However, our χmax\chi_{\rm max} has the same size dependence, regardless of being a ground state or excited states, which is because their construction is formally the same. It therefore appears that the area and volume law difference comes from the distribution of Schmidt values within the same χmax\chi_{\rm max}.

The big advantage of our TN description is that the Schmidt states are available. With this, one can show that the post-projection states with different quantum numbers do not fully share the Schmidt state, or in other words, the Majorana fermions are quasi-local. (See Appendix C for mathematical proof).

III.3 Topological order

III.3.1 Schmidt values

Following our numerical observation on the reduction of the Schmidt states, we analytically show that the constraint Di=1D_{i}=1 supported by 𝒫D{\cal P}_{D} creates a topological term of EE. Let us first rewrite the fermionic eigenstate using the ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} bond gauge |𝒖⟩|\bm{u}\rangle and fermionic part |M𝒖⟩|M_{\bm{u}}\rangle explicitly as |Ψ~𝒖,𝒗M⟩=|𝒖⟩​|M𝒖⟩|\tilde{\Psi}^{M}_{\bm{u},\bm{v}}\rangle=|\bm{u}\rangle|M_{\bm{u}}\rangle. As we bipartite it to 𝒜{\cal A} and ℬ{\cal B} along the closed loop, which cuts totally 2​L2L different ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} bonds (Fig. 2(e)), the 2​L2L different bond gauges are rearranged in a way that they reconnect and form boundary gauge operators w^𝒜,n=i​b^𝒜,2​n−1α​b^𝒜,2​nβ\hat{w}_{{\cal A},n}=i\hat{b}^{\alpha}_{{\cal A},2n-1}\hat{b}^{\beta}_{{\cal A},2n} and w^ℬ,n=i​b^ℬ,2​n−1α​b^ℬ,2​nβ\hat{w}_{{\cal B},n}=i\hat{b}^{\alpha}_{{\cal B},2n-1}\hat{b}^{\beta}_{{\cal B},2n}, whose eigenvalues rely on |u2​n−1,u2​n⟩=|±,1±1⟩|u_{2n-1},u_{2n}\rangle=|\pm,1\pm 1\rangle and |∓1,±1⟩|\mp 1,\pm 1\rangle on the cut as |w𝒜,n,wℬ,n⟩=(|−1,1⟩±|1,−1⟩)/2|w_{{\cal A},n},w_{{\cal B},n}\rangle=(|-1,1\rangle\pm|1,-1\rangle)/\sqrt{2} and (|1,1⟩±|−1,−1⟩)/2(|1,1\rangle\pm|-1,-1\rangle)/\sqrt{2}, each confined inside the region 𝒜{\cal A} or ℬ{\cal B}. Accordingly, the gauge states are divided as |𝒖⟩=|𝒖𝒜⟩​|w𝒜⟩​|𝒖ℬ⟩​|wℬ⟩|\bm{u}\rangle=|\bm{u}^{\cal A}\rangle|w^{\cal A}\rangle|\bm{u}^{\cal B}\rangle|w^{\cal B}\rangle, where |𝒖ℛ⟩|\bm{u}^{\cal R}\rangle are the ones inside region ℛ=𝒜,ℬ{\cal R}={\cal A},{\cal B} that do not touch the cut, and |wℛ⟩|w^{\cal R}\rangle are the boundary gauge states; these facts are known so far[25]. Since |Ψ~𝒖,𝒗M⟩|\tilde{\Psi}^{M}_{\bm{u},\bm{v}}\rangle is the product of gauge and matter part, the latter is trivially Schmidt decomposed into |M𝒖​ℓ𝒜⟩​|M𝒖​ℓℬ⟩|M^{\cal A}_{\bm{u}\ell}\rangle|M^{\cal B}_{\bm{u}\ell}\rangle and we obtain an explicit Schmidt form,

Consequently, the 2L−12^{L-1} degeneracy remains in the projected Schmidt spectrum, with each λℓ\lambda_{\ell} multiplied by 2\sqrt{2}, providing an analytical proof of Fig. 2(d). Previously, the explicit form of the EE was obtained by Yao and Qi as S=(L−1)​ln⁡2+α​LS=(L-1)\ln 2+\alpha L, by calculating the trace of the local density matrix using a Replica trick 33 3 In Ref.[25], they directly constructed the density operator ρ𝒜\cal\rho_{\cal A} of the post-projected state consisting of equal-weight superposition of different gauge configurations. The form of ρ𝒜\cal\rho_{\cal A} includes the nontrivial off-diagonal contributions between different gauge configurations that seem highly nontrivial to reconcile with the Schmidt decomposition. Instead, they directly evaluated Tr𝒜​((ρ𝒜)n){\rm Tr}_{\cal A}\big((\rho_{\cal A})^{n}\big), integrated over the regions 𝒜{\cal A}, and applied the Replica trick to obtain the von Neumann entropy. See Appendix B.2 for details. . Here, we disclosed the complete entanglement structure under the gauge constraint, namely, at the quantum many-body level for spin Hamiltonian, and showed how it generates −ln⁡2-\ln 2. There is another complementary study by Dóra and Moessner[41] that confines itself to the quantum many-body spin Hamiltonian, or equivalently to its Jordan-Wigner fermionic form, successfully separating the gauge and matter sectors and integrating the latter, showing that the zero-flux sector of the ground state alone could generate a −ln⁡2-\ln 2 term, which gives a good connection to the cylinder DMRG.

III.3.2 Gauge constraint

With in mind that the D=1D=1 constraint to the Majorana fermions plays a crucial role in generating −ln⁡2-\ln 2 at post-projection, we reexamine the formula [37, 38, 39],

D=(−)Nx+N/2​sgn​(Pf⁡(A))​∏⟨j,k⟩uj,k​(−)∑ℓ=1N/2n^ℓ,D=(-)^{N_{x}+N/2}{\rm sgn}\big({\rm Pf}(A)\big)\prod_{\langle j,k\rangle}u_{j,k}(-)^{\sum_{\ell=1}^{N/2}\hat{n}_{\ell}},\vskip-5.69054pt (12)

by expressing it using the sign of the Pfaffian. To understand its implication, we consider a bond-randomized version of Eq.(1) with Jγ=1+Δj​kJ_{\gamma}=1+\Delta_{jk}, where Δj​k\Delta_{jk} follows the uniformly random distribution at [−Δ:Δ][-\Delta:\Delta]. Figure 3(a) shows the signed fraction of sgn⁡(Pf⁡(A)){\rm sgn}\big({\rm Pf}(A)\big); the emergent sgn⁡(Pf⁡(A))=1{\rm sgn}\big({\rm Pf}(A)\big)=1 signals the gap closing associated with the condensation of the random flux state, predicted to occur near Δ∼0.96\Delta\sim 0.96[42]. Its Schmidt spectrum is exactly halved by 𝒫D{\cal P}_{D} (see the inset), showing that the disordered eigenstates remain topologically ordered irrespective of sgn⁡(Pf⁡(A))=±1{\rm sgn}\big({\rm Pf}(A)\big)=\pm 1.

While the Pfaffian serves as a ℤ2{\mathbb{Z}}_{2} topological invariant in the quantum spin Hall effect [43, 44], the present case is more closely related to the Pfaffian invariant of the Kitaev chain, where it signals the U(1) symmetry breaking into the topological superconductor supporting unpaired Majorana edge modes [45]. This correspondence suggests that our framework naturally extends to general parton Hamiltonians and has similarity to the Kitaev chain.

III.4 Quasi-localized Majorana fermions

The Schmidt vectors encode the purely quantum many-body aspects of the QSL state. We divide the system into 𝒜=1,⋯,k{\cal A}={1,\cdots,k} and ℬ=k+1,⋯,N{\cal B}={k+1,\cdots,N}, and Schmidt-decompose the rrth (=𝒖,𝒏{\bm{u},\bm{n}}) eigenstate as

|Ψr⟩=∑s=1χλs​|ψr,s𝒜⟩​|ϕr,sℬ⟩,|{\Psi}_{r}\rangle=\sum_{s=1}^{\chi}\lambda_{s}|\psi_{r,s}^{{\cal A}}\rangle|\phi_{r,s}^{{\cal B}}\rangle, (13)

where χ\chi is the number of nonzero Schmidt values. We define the subspace associated with the rrth eigenstate as 𝒱k,r𝒜=span​{|ψr,s𝒜⟩}s=1χ{\cal V}_{k,r}^{{\cal A}}={\rm span}\{|\psi_{r,s}^{{\cal A}}\rangle\}_{s=1}^{\chi}. Comparing two arbitrary states rr and r′r^{\prime}, we find that if 𝒱k,r(𝒜)∩𝒱k,r′(𝒜)=0{\cal V}_{k,r}^{({\cal A})}\cap{\cal V}_{k,r^{\prime}}^{({\cal A})}=0, their Schmidt subspaces have no overlap in region 𝒜{\cal A}.

Starting from k=Nk=N, we decrease kk until the overlap becomes nonzero. We define the “kk-local” scale as the maximum size of 𝒜{\cal A} for which the two states share nontrivial local quantum states. If the states belong to different quantum-number sectors, 𝒖r≠𝒖r′\bm{u}_{r}\neq\bm{u}_{r^{\prime}}, then kk is always smaller than the corresponding region size, and the states are trivially orthogonal. We therefore focus on pairs of states in the same 𝒖\bm{u} sector and plot kr​r′k_{rr^{\prime}} in Fig. 3(b). For the Kitaev honeycomb model, states are ordered from left to right by the binary representation of the fermion occupation numbers (n1n2⋯nN/2;2n_{1}n_{2}\cdots n_{N/2;2}), while for the other models, they are ordered by energy. The similarities between fermionic states differ markedly from those between the corresponding physical states after projection. For comparison, we perform the same analysis for the classical Ising, XX, Heisenberg (XXX), and XYZ spin chains, using all eigenstates for N=10−13N=10-13. For the XYZ model, we set Jx=1J_{x}=1, Jy=1.53J_{y}=1.53, and Jz=1.79J_{z}=1.79 in the Hamiltonian HXYZ=∑γ=x,y,z∑i=1NJγ​Siγ​Si+1γH_{{\rm XYZ}}=\sum_{\gamma=x,y,z}\sum_{i=1}^{N}J_{\gamma}S^{\gamma}_{i}S^{\gamma}_{i+1}. Compared with the Kitaev honeycomb model, the resulting density plots for these standard models exhibit relatively structureless patterns.

To quantify kk-localness, we plot the distribution of kr​r′/Nk_{rr^{\prime}}/N over all pairs (r,r′)(r,r^{\prime}) within the flux-free sector in Fig. 3(c). The Ising model exhibits a peak at k=0k=0, with a distribution that decays exponentially with increasing kk, reflecting the 2N−k2^{N-k} scaling of the number of kk-local states. In contrast, the other quantum spin chains exhibit peaks at k=Nk=N, followed by exponential decay as kk decreases. This behavior may reflect the quantum correlations in these quantum-critical states, which arise from superpositions of similar states. The kk-localness of the Kitaev spin liquid, however, differs distinctly from both the Ising and other quantum spin states. The distribution vanishes for k≳0.9​Nk\gtrsim 0.9N and k≤0.5​Nk\leq 0.5N. The latter feature is attributed to the nonlocal Majorana fermionic wave function, which extends over more than half the system. Although the fermionic solutions of the Kitaev honeycomb model retain a nonzero component near k=Nk=N, their distribution differs from those of the other quantum states. This component vanishes upon projection onto the physical states. Physically, this result indicates that the spin-liquid states do not share a common global basis set within the sector. This feature can be understood by analogy with a Rokhsar–Kivelson state[46], an analytical realization of a ℤ2{\mathbb{Z}}_{2} spin liquid. Such a state is an equal-weight superposition of dimer coverings, and distinct basis states exhibit k<Nk<N-locality. These results establish kk-localness as a fingerprint for identifying topological order in the quantum many-body framework. Indeed, the Kitaev honeycomb state exhibits a similar structure through the equal-weight superposition of DgD_{g}-operated states in Eq. (27).

The spatial distribution of each Majorana fermion that constitutes the spin liquid ground state and excited states is also solved analytically (see Appendix C), and the maximum range that the fermions could spread is restricted to ∼3/4\sim 3/4 of the system size, which is consistent with the numerical observation of kk-local in Fig. 3(c).

IV Parton theory

IV.1 Parton Hamiltonian

To generalize our central findings to the QSL realized in other quantum spin models, we consider a mean-field parton Hamiltonian, which gives the basic description of the QSL obtained by the variational Monte Carlo studies. We start from the S=1/2S=1/2 quantum Heisenberg model given as, ℋ=J​∑⟨i,j⟩𝑺i⋅𝑺j{\cal H}=J\sum_{\langle i,j\rangle}{\bm{S}}_{i}\cdot{\bm{S}}_{j}, and rewrite the spin operator using the Abrikosov fermion fi​σf_{i\sigma} as

𝑺i=12​fi​σ†​𝝈α​β​fi​β,∑σfi​σ†​fi​σ=1,\displaystyle{\bm{S}}_{i}=\frac{1}{2}f_{i\sigma}^{\dagger}\bm{\sigma}_{\alpha\beta}f_{i\beta},\quad\sum_{\sigma}f_{i\sigma}^{\dagger}f_{i\sigma}=1, (14)

which gives the form,

ℋp0=J4​∑⟨i,j⟩fi​σ†​fi​β​fj​σ†​fj​β​𝝈α​β⋅𝝈α​β.\displaystyle{\cal H}_{p}^{0}=\frac{J}{4}\sum_{\langle i,j\rangle}f_{i\sigma}^{\dagger}f_{i\beta}f_{j\sigma}^{\dagger}f_{j\beta}\bm{\sigma}_{\alpha\beta}\cdot\bm{\sigma}_{\alpha\beta}. (15)

By introducing the mean-field as χi​j=2​⟨fj​σ†​fi​σ⟩\chi_{ij}=2\langle f_{j\sigma}^{\dagger}f_{i\sigma}\rangle, Δi​j=⟨−fi↑​fj↓+fi↓​fj↑⟩\Delta_{ij}=\langle-f_{i\uparrow}f_{j\downarrow}+f_{i\downarrow}f_{j\uparrow}\rangle, we find the parton Hamiltonian,

ℋp=\displaystyle{\cal H}_{p}= ∑⟨i,j⟩(∑σ=↑,↓χi​jfi​σ†fj​σ+Δi​j(fi↑†fj↓†+h.c.))\displaystyle\sum_{\langle i,j\rangle}\Big(\sum_{\sigma=\uparrow,\downarrow}\chi_{ij}f_{i\sigma}^{\dagger}f_{j\sigma}+\Delta_{ij}\big(f^{\dagger}_{i\uparrow}f^{\dagger}_{j\downarrow}+h.c.\big)\Big)
+∑i(∑σ=↑,↓μfi​σ†fi​σ+ζ(fi↑†fi↓†+h.c.))\displaystyle+\sum_{i}\Big(\sum_{\sigma=\uparrow,\downarrow}\mu f_{i\sigma}^{\dagger}f_{i\sigma}+\zeta\big(f^{\dagger}_{i\uparrow}f^{\dagger}_{i\downarrow}+h.c.\big)\Big) (16)

After obtaining the eigenstate of this Hamiltonian, |ΨMF⟩|\Psi_{\rm MF}\rangle, one needs to transform it to the spin space, which is done by the Gutzwiller projection, PG=∏i(ni↑−ni↓)2P_{G}=\prod_{i}(n_{i\uparrow}-n_{i\downarrow})^{2}, with ni​σ=fi​σ†​fi​σn_{i\sigma}=f_{i\sigma}^{\dagger}f_{i\sigma}, and the resultant |ΨSL⟩=PG​|ΨMF⟩|\Psi_{\rm SL}\rangle=P_{G}|\Psi_{\rm MF}\rangle is considered as a good ansatz for the spin liquid state realized in the original Heisenberg model.

IV.2 Gauge operators

The Majorana fermions corresponding to the Abrikosov fermions are given as

ci​σ;1=fi​σ+fi​σ†,ci​σ;2=(−i)​(fi​σ−fi​σ†).\displaystyle c_{i\sigma;1}=f_{i\sigma}+f^{\dagger}_{i\sigma},\quad c_{i\sigma;2}=(-i)(f_{i\sigma}-f^{\dagger}_{i\sigma}). (17)

We introduce an operator

D^i=ci↑;1​ci↑;2​ci↓;1​ci↓;2.\displaystyle\hat{D}_{i}=c_{i\uparrow;1}c_{i\uparrow;2}c_{i\downarrow;1}c_{i\downarrow;2}. (18)

Since D^i\hat{D}_{i} commutes with 𝑺i{\bm{S}}_{i} for all ii, it is a conserved quantity for the spin Hamiltonian, or equivalently, ℋp0{\cal H}_{p}^{0} in Eq.(15). The eigenstates of the spin Hamiltonian are indexed by {Di=±1}i=1N\{D_{i}=\pm 1\}_{i=1}^{N}. When the eigenstate of ℋp0{\cal H}_{p}^{0} is obtained, it is put back into the spin space by the Gutzwiller projection, where only the Di=1,∀iD_{i}=1,\,^{\forall}i component remains as the true ground state of the original Heisenberg model. However, the introduction of mean-field in Eq.(16) breaks this local conservation, as D^i\hat{D}_{i} no longer commutes with ℋp{\cal H}_{p}. Since μ\mu in the mean-field Hamiltonian is set to keep the system half-filled, the expectation values of the following operators evaluated by their ground state |Ψf(MF)⟩|\Psi_{f}^{(\rm MF)}\rangle satisfy,

⟨fi​σ†​fi​σ⟩=12,⟨fi↑†​fi↓⟩=⟨fi↓†​fi↑⟩=0.\displaystyle\langle f^{\dagger}_{i\sigma}f_{i\sigma}\rangle=\frac{1}{2},\quad\langle f^{\dagger}_{i\uparrow}f_{i\downarrow}\rangle=\langle f^{\dagger}_{i\downarrow}f_{i\uparrow}\rangle=0. (19)

Here, we used ⟨fi​σ†​fi​σ+fi​σ​fi​σ†⟩=1\langle f^{\dagger}_{i\sigma}f_{i\sigma}+f_{i\sigma}f^{\dagger}_{i\sigma}\rangle=1. Accordingly, ⟨cja​cjb⟩=0\langle c_{j}^{a}c_{j}^{b}\rangle=0 is satisfied for all a≠ba\neq b, a,b=(α,σ)a,b=(\alpha,\sigma) with α=1,2\alpha=1,2, σ=↑,↓\sigma=\uparrow,\downarrow. Wick’s theorem naturally gives,

⟨D^i⟩\displaystyle\langle\hat{D}_{i}\rangle =⟨ci↑;1​ci↑;2⟩​⟨ci↓;1​ci↓;2⟩−⟨ci↑;1​ci↑;2⟩​⟨ci↓;1​ci↓;2⟩\displaystyle=\langle c_{i\uparrow;1}c_{i\uparrow;2}\rangle\langle c_{i\downarrow;1}c_{i\downarrow;2}\rangle-\langle c_{i\uparrow;1}c_{i\uparrow;2}\rangle\langle c_{i\downarrow;1}c_{i\downarrow;2}\rangle
+⟨ci↑;1​ci↓;2⟩​⟨ci↑;2​ci↓;1⟩\displaystyle\quad+\langle c_{i\uparrow;1}c_{i\downarrow;2}\rangle\langle c_{i\uparrow;2}c_{i\downarrow;1}\rangle
=0,\displaystyle=0, (20)

for the mean-field state that has equal probability of Di=±1D_{i}=\pm 1.

The global projector is constructed as

D^=∏i=1ND^i,\displaystyle\hat{D}=\prod_{i=1}^{N}\hat{D}_{i}, (21)

Unlike the local operator, D^\hat{D} commutes with ℋp{\cal H}_{p}, so that |Ψf(MF)⟩|\Psi_{f}^{(\rm MF)}\rangle is an eigenstate of D^\hat{D}, where only the D=1D=1 value is allowed for fermions, because D=−1D=-1 does not survive after the Gutzwiller approximation. Accordingly, as has been done previously for the Kitaev-honeycomb case in Eqs.(26) and (27), we are able to expand the post-projection wave function as,

|Ψf(MF)⟩=12N−1​∑{Di},D=1|Ψf,{Di}⟩,|\Psi_{f}^{(\rm MF)}\rangle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2^{N-1}}}\sum_{\{D_{i}\},D=1}|\Psi_{f,\{D_{i}\}}\rangle, (22)

where |Ψf,{Di}⟩|\Psi_{f,\{D_{i}\}}\rangle is the possible or approximate eigenstate of ℋp0{\cal H}_{p}^{0} before taking a mean-field, where each Di=±1D_{i}=\pm 1 is well defined.

The nontrivial point for the general parton theory is that, unlike the Kitaev honeycomb model, |Ψf,{Di}⟩|\Psi_{f,\{D_{i}\}}\rangle is not necessarily written as the product of gauge and matter parts, which does not allow the discussions we expanded in Sec. III.3.1 and App. B.2. However, because the global gauge operator in region 𝒜{\cal A}, D^𝒜=∏j=1N𝒜D^j\hat{D}_{\cal A}=\prod_{j=1}^{N_{\cal A}}\hat{D}_{j}, also commutes the fermion parity operator in region 𝒜{\cal A} (see Eq.(51)), similarly to Eq.(40), the Schmidt state in 𝒜{\cal A} is an eigenstate of D^𝒜\hat{D}_{\cal A}. This fact allows us to expand the parallel discussions on the Schmidt decomposition we made for the Kitaev-honeycomb model. The parton Hamiltonian therefore contains no explicit ℤ2{\mathbb{Z}}_{2} gauge variables.

This D^\hat{D} has the same form as Eq.(12), except that the bond-gauge factor ∏uj,k\prod u_{j,k} is absent. When Δi​j=ζ=0\Delta_{ij}=\zeta=0, the spin-up and down fermions remain decoupled, and sgn⁡[Pf⁡(A)]=1{\rm sgn}[{\rm Pf}(A)]=1, so that the Pfaffian does not enter D^\hat{D}. After the Gutzwiller projection, this corresponds to a U(1) spin liquid for appropriate Δi​j\Delta_{ij}, By contrast, finite pairing Δi​j≠0\Delta_{ij}\neq 0 introduces the factor sgn⁡[Pf⁡(A)]=±1{\rm sgn}[{\rm Pf}(A)]=\pm 1 into D^\hat{D}, yielding a ℤ2{\mathbb{Z}}_{2} spin liquid. The Pfaffian therefore encodes the breaking of the U(1) gauge symmetry (Appendix D.1).

IV.3 Kagome antiferromagnet

To show that the projection-induced topological order is not specific to the Kitaev honeycomb model, we analyze the U(1) and ℤ2{\mathbb{Z}}_{2} parton wave functions proposed for the kagome Heisenberg model [48] (Appendix D.3). As shown in the inset of Fig. 4, χi​j\chi_{ij} between the nearest and next-nearest neighbors, second nearest neighbor Δi​j\Delta_{ij}, and on-site ζ>0\zeta>0 are considered, where both χi​j\chi_{ij} and Δi​j\Delta_{ij} take plus and minus distributions. Figure 4(a) shows the Rényi-2 entropy S2S_{2} on a YC cylinder as a function of the circumference cc, the choice allowing direct comparison with the DMRG results for the ℤ2{\mathbb{Z}}_{2} spin liquid [47]. The ℤ2{\mathbb{Z}}_{2} parton state exhibits nearly half the S2S_{2} of the U(1) state, which is understood in analogy with the Kitaev chain [45]; in the fermionic language, the superconducting pairing in the ℤ2{\mathbb{Z}}_{2} state halves the number of free particles, and hence their entanglement arising from their distribution is halved.

Remarkably, the unprojected ℤ2{\mathbb{Z}}_{2} parton state follows the almost the same linear scaling as the DMRG spin state, except for the constant −ln⁡2-\ln 2 shift: Here, notice that the linear line for DMRG is taken from Ref.[47], and the fitting curve of our data for the ℤ2{\mathbb{Z}}_{2} parton theory gives the slope with zero intercept. Microscopically, the Schmidt spectrum separates into two nearly degenerate sectors with D𝒜=±1D_{\cal A}=\pm 1 (Fig. 4(b)), and the projection removes the D𝒜=−1D_{\cal A}=-1 sector, which we have proved analytically in Sec. IV.2 as the outcome of the commutativity of D^𝒜\hat{D}_{\cal A} and 𝒫D{\cal P}_{D}. Similar behavior is found for the J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} triangular-lattice antiferromagnet (see Fig. 8). As neither the Heisenberg models nor the parton Hamiltonian contains explicit bond-gauge variables, these results identify the post-projection collapse of the fermionic into spin state by the gauge constraint as a generic bulk signature of topological order. It is a bulk counterpart to the Wilson-loop characterization of topological order proposed by Levin and Wen [26, 27], establishing a bulk-boundary correspondence between the gauge constraint inside the wave function and the universal topological contribution to the EE.

V Concluding remarks

We have established an exact tensor-network representation of the full set of eigenstates of the Kitaev honeycomb model for sufficiently large systems to accurately capture their entanglement properties. The complete Schmidt decomposition reveals that the Schmidt eigenvalues and corresponding eigenstates are reduced by half when a fermionic eigenstate undergoes Gutzwiller projection onto the physical spin Hilbert space. This reduction accounts for the universal −ln⁡2-\ln 2 contribution to the entanglement entropy associated with topological order.

There are two remarks. First, since the topological contribution, at least for the gapped QSL, is taken as a key signature of a QSL, the unprojected Majorana fermion states are not the QSL state; the physical spin-liquid character emerges only after Gutzwiller projection. Second, this halving of the Schmidt spectrum occurs exactly for every eigenstate, indicating that the same topological entanglement contribution persists throughout the spectrum, including in excited states.

The mechanism underlying this halving is demonstrated by the exact analytical form of the Schmidt decomposition, using the global gauge operator D^\hat{D}, defined as the product of the local gauge operators D^i\hat{D}_{i} over all sites. Since D^\hat{D} commutes with both the Majorana and spin Hamiltonians, its eigenvalue is factorized into those of subsystems AA and BB, with D=DA​DB=1D=D_{A}D_{B}=1 and DA,DB=±1D_{A},D_{B}=\pm 1. The Gutzwiller projection, which imposes the local constraints Di=1D_{i}=1 to reduce the enlarged Majorana Hilbert space to the physical spin Hilbert space, selects the DA=DB=1D_{A}=D_{B}=1 sector. Importantly, this fact is rigorous, since the Gutzwiller projector commutes with both D^A\hat{D}_{A}, D^B\hat{D}_{B}. This constraint provides an analytical explanation for the reduction of the Schmidt spectrum by half and the resulting −ln⁡2-\ln 2 contribution to the entanglement entropy.

At first sight, this mechanism might appear to be a special feature of the exactly solvable Kitaev honeycomb model. However, we find that the same formulation of the gauge operator D^\hat{D} applies to the Abrikosov-fermion parton mean-field theory, a standard framework for describing QSLs in the S=1/2S=1/2 Heisenberg model. Guided by this observation, we investigate mean-field parton states of the kagome Heisenberg model using parameters obtained from previous variational Monte Carlo studies. The resulting Schmidt spectra exhibit near-degenerate sectors associated with DA=±1D_{A}=\pm 1, and the Gutzwiller projection is performed independently of the sectors, rigorously eliminating the −1-1 component. This finding suggests that selecting one of these sectors through Gutzwiller projection provides a microscopic origin for the topological entanglement contribution. However, an explicit Gutzwiller projection of the parton mean-field states for sufficiently large systems is not currently available. Indeed, previous VMC works show that the precise evaluation of the topological term, γ\gamma, with the Gutzwiller projection may suffer numerical difficulty, which can vary from γ=0.584±0.089\gamma=0.584\pm 0.089[49] to 0.288±0.1070.288\pm 0.107[50], and γ=0.2±0.04\gamma=0.2\pm 0.04[51] , even using the same scheme of evaluation. This fact highlights the utmost difficulty of even simply extracting the −ln⁡2-\ln 2 term and performing the proper Gutzwiller projection to the quantum many-body level, which requires numerically exact schemes even with the limited system sizes. The application of the exact TN method to more general QSL states, in order to clarify the role of Gutzwiller projection to the general QSL needs further investigation.

Still, our findings provide a microscopic perspective on how gauge constraints shape the entanglement structure of QSL, extending previous loop-based approaches to a framework that directly connects gauge sectors with the Schmidt spectrum. More broadly, our results establish a basis for investigating how the gauge structure of parton representations determines the entanglement properties of physical spin states.

Appendix A Details of exact tensor-network solutions

A.1 Conserved quantities

In the Kitaev honeycomb spin Hamiltonian Eq.(1), there are N/2+1N/2+1 independent conserved quantities: the N/2N/2 plaquettes Wp=∏i∈ℒpσiαiW_{p}=\prod_{i\in{\cal L}_{p}}\sigma_{i}^{\alpha_{i}} and the two loop operators Wx=∏i∈ℒxσiαiW_{x}=\prod_{i\in{\cal L}_{x}}\sigma_{i}^{\alpha_{i}}, Wy=∏i∈ℒyσiαiW_{y}=\prod_{i\in{\cal L}_{y}}\sigma_{i}^{\alpha_{i}} where ℒp{\cal L}_{p} is a loop around the plaquette pp and ℒx,y{\cal L}_{x,y} are loops around the torus in the x,yx,y directions. αi=x,y,z\alpha_{i}=x,y,z is the bond index connnected to site ii but is not included in the loop. Since ∏pWp=1\prod_{p}W_{p}=1, the number of independent quantities decreases by one, and the Hilbert space has 2N/2+12^{N/2+1} independent sectors of dimension 2N/2−12^{N/2-1}.

The conserved quantities w={{wp},wx,wy}=w=\{\{w_{p}\},w_{x},w_{y}\}= 1 or −1-1 are the product of uj​ku_{jk} on the loop. We note that since |Ψ~u,n⟩|\tilde{\Psi}_{u,n}\rangle is an eigenstate of D^=∏i=1ND^i\hat{D}=\prod_{i=1}^{N}\hat{D}_{i}, 𝒖,𝒏\bm{u},\bm{n} needs to satisfy D^=1\hat{D}=1 to obtain a physical state[39, 37], where DD is explicitly written as [39]

D=∏i=1NDi=(−1)Nx​det⁡Qr​∏l=1N/2(1−2​nl)​∏⟨j,k⟩uj​k,D=\prod_{i=1}^{N}D_{i}=(-1)^{N_{x}}\det Q_{r}\prod_{l=1}^{N/2}(1-2n_{l})\prod_{\langle j,k\rangle}u_{jk}, (23)

where Qr=2​[Re​Q1,Im​Q1,⋯,Re​QN/2,Im​QN/2]Q_{r}=\sqrt{2}[{\rm Re}Q_{1},{\rm Im}Q_{1},\cdots,{\rm Re}Q_{N/2},{\rm Im}Q_{N/2}] is an orthogonal matrix, whose columns are the real and imaginary parts of half the columns of QQ used to diagonalize the free Majorana, Q=[Q1,⋯,QN]Q=[Q_{1},\cdots,Q_{N}].

By converting det⁡Qr=(−)N/2​sgn​(Pf⁡(A))\det Q_{r}=(-)^{N/2}\mathrm{sgn}(\mathrm{Pf}(A)), we obtain the explicit form Eq.(12). Here, we briefly explain its derivation. Because the antisymmetric matrix AA is block-diagonalized as Qrt​A​QrQ_{r}^{t}AQ_{r}, with ∓ϵℓ\mp\epsilon_{\ell} forming an off-diagonal element of each ℓ=1,⋯,N/2\ell=1,\cdots,N/2 block matrices,

Pf⁡(Qrt​A​Qr)=(−)N/2​∏ℓ=1N/2ϵℓ=(−)N/2​det⁡A,\displaystyle\mathrm{Pf}(Q_{r}^{t}AQ_{r})=(-)^{N/2}\prod_{\ell=1}^{N/2}\epsilon_{\ell}=(-)^{N/2}\sqrt{\det A}, (24)

where det⁡(i​A)=(∏ℓ=1N/2ϵℓ)(∏ℓ=1N/2−ϵℓ)\det(iA)=(\prod_{\ell=1}^{N/2}\epsilon_{\ell})(\prod_{\ell=1}^{N/2}-\epsilon_{\ell}). Using the formula Pf⁡(Qrt​A​Qr)=det⁡(Qr)​Pf​(A)\mathrm{Pf}(Q_{r}^{t}AQ_{r})=\det(Q_r)\mathrm{Pf}(A), we obtain

det⁡(Qr)=(−)N/2​det⁡A/Pf⁡(A)=(−)N/2​sgn​(Pf⁡(A)).\displaystyle\det(Q_r)=(-)^{N/2}\sqrt{\det A}/\mathrm{Pf}(A)=(-)^{N/2}\mathrm{sgn}(\mathrm{Pf}(A)). (25)

A.2 Distribution of singular values

We discussed in the main text that for all the TN exact solutions, the bond dimension χm\chi_{m} which is the number of nonzero Schmidt coefficients is the same regardless of whether it is the ground state or the excited state (for any given quantum numbers 𝒖,𝒏\bm{u},\bm{n}). Figure 5 shows the distribution of nonzero singular values λq\lambda_{q} when we Schmidt-decompose the state by the bipartition to 𝒜={1,⋯,m}{\cal A}=\{1,\cdots,m\} and ℬ={m+1,⋯,N}{\cal B}=\{m+1,\cdots,N\} where we set m=N/2m=N/2. Two distinct features are observed. For all values of λq\lambda_{q}, the degeneracy is twice as large for the fermionic eigenstate, |Ψ~𝒖,𝒏M⟩|\tilde{\Psi}^{M}_{\bm{u},\bm{n}}\rangle, while the corresponding λq\lambda_{q}’s of the physical eigenstate |Ψ𝒖,𝒏⟩|\Psi_{\bm{u},\bm{n}}\rangle is reduced, λq→2​λq\lambda_{q}\rightarrow\sqrt{2}\lambda_{q}. Namely, by scaling the horizontal and vertical axes by ×2\times 2 and /2/\sqrt{2}, the two data lines exactly collapse.

The second feature is that although the maximum number of Schmidt values χm\chi_{m} is the same between the ground and excited states, the values of λq\lambda_{q} are more widely spread for the latter, which yields a volume-law entanglement.

A.3 Volume law of the excited states

In Fig. 2(a) in the main text, we showed the entanglement entropy for N=32N=32 of the MPS-MPO solution, where we argued that the volume law behavior is observed for the excited state solutions in contrast to the ground state, although the bond dimensions are the same. To further support our claim, we show in Fig. 6(a) the entanglement entropy of the same N=2​Nx×Ny=2×4×4N=2N_{x}\times N_{y}=2\times 4\times 4 cluster as a function of N𝒜=2​Nx𝒜​Ny𝒜N_{\cal A}=2N_{x}^{\cal A}N_{y}^{\cal A} (the number of sites included in 𝒜{\cal A}), where we set Ny𝒜=4N_{y}^{\cal A}=4 constant and vary Nx𝒜N_{x}^{\cal A}. The results do not contradict the volume law.

For clarification, we show in Fig. 6(b) the case of Nx=Ny=64N_{x}=N_{y}=64 that amounts to N=8192N=8192, with the region 𝒜{\cal A} taken as in the inset, keeping the aspect ratio to 1 in the xx and yy directions; N𝒜=n2N_{\cal A}=n^{2} with the boundary length given as L=3​nL=3n. We compare the case of the entanglement entropy of the matter fermions, S𝒜m=∑ℓλℓ2​ln⁡λℓ2S_{\cal A}^{m}=\sum_{\ell}\lambda^{2}_{\ell}\ln\lambda_{\ell}^{2}, that of the Majorana fermions, S𝒜f=L​ln⁡2+S𝒜mS_{\cal A}^{f}=L\ln 2+S_{\cal A}^{m}, and the physical ones after the Gutzwiller projection, S𝒜p=(L−1)​ln⁡2+S𝒜mS_{\cal A}^{p}=(L-1)\ln 2+S_{\cal A}^{m}. The difference, S𝒜p−S𝒜f=−ln⁡2S_{\cal A}^{p}-S_{\cal A}^{f}=-\ln 2, is almost invisible for the scale of the figure, while it is present and supports the topological order. With this result, one finds that the volume law is safely distinguished at N𝒜≳600N_{\cal A}\gtrsim 600, and is present for larger NN. We also notice that the matter fermion part, S𝒜mS_{\cal A}^{m} is mainly responsible for the volume-law behavior of the excited states of the Kitaev honeycomb model.

Appendix B Gutzwiller projection

B.1 Gauge constraint and post-projection state.

Let us illustrate the nature of the post-projection state. The fermionic state is an eigenstate of D^=∏i=1ND^i\hat{D}=\prod_{i=1}^{N}\hat{D}_{i} but is not the eigenstate of D^i\hat{D}_{i}. The operator 𝒫D{\cal P}_{D} in Eq.(3) projects it to the simultaneous eigenstates of all D^i\hat{D}_{i}’s and is expanded as

𝒫D=∏j=1N1+D^j2=12N​∑gD^g,D^g=∏j∈gD^j,\displaystyle{\cal P}_{D}=\prod_{j=1}^{N}\frac{1+\hat{D}_{j}}{2}=\frac{1}{2^{N}}\sum_{g}\hat{D}_{g},\quad\hat{D}_{g}=\prod_{j\in g}\hat{D}_{j}, (26)

where gg runs over all the subsets of lattice sites, chosen from among all the lattice sites ℒ{\mathcal{L}}. Because the condition D^​|Ψ~𝒖,𝒏M⟩=|Ψ~𝒖,𝒏M⟩\hat{D}|\tilde{\Psi}^{M}_{\bm{u},\bm{n}}\rangle=|\tilde{\Psi}^{M}_{\bm{u},\bm{n}}\rangle, is rewritten as D^g​|Ψ~𝒖,𝒏M⟩=D^ℒ−g​|Ψ~𝒖,𝒏M⟩\hat{D}_{g}|\tilde{\Psi}^{M}_{\bm{u},\bm{n}}\rangle=\hat{D}_{{\mathcal{L}}-g}|\tilde{\Psi}^{M}_{\bm{u},\bm{n}}\rangle, among the 2N2^{N} terms in ∑g\sum_{g}, only half are independent. The normalization factor of the post-projected state needs to be multiplied by 1/21/\sqrt{2} to reduce this redundancy:

|Ψ𝒖,𝒏⟩\displaystyle|\Psi_{\bm{u},\bm{n}}\rangle =12N+1​∑gD^g​|Ψ~𝒖,𝒏M⟩,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2^{N+1}}}\sum_{g}\hat{D}_{g}|\tilde{\Psi}^{M}_{\bm{u},\bm{n}}\rangle, (27)

which ends up with the equal-weight superposition of 2N−12^{N-1} independent states gauge-transformed by different D^g\hat{D}_{g}’s [25]. These discussions rephrase those in Refs.[37, 39, 25].

To prepare for the next subsection, we now divide the system into 𝒜{\cal A} and ℬ{\cal B}. Here, the projection operator, 𝒫D{\cal P}_{D}, is naturally divided into those operating on the two as 𝒫D=𝒫D𝒜​𝒫Dℬ{\cal P}_{D}={\cal P}_{D}^{\cal A}{\cal P}_{D}^{\cal B}, with

𝒫D𝒜=∏j=1N𝒜1+D^j2=12N𝒜​∑g∈𝒜D^g,D^g=∏j∈gD^j.\displaystyle{\cal P}_{D}^{\cal A}=\prod_{j=1}^{N_{\cal A}}\frac{1+\hat{D}_{j}}{2}=\frac{1}{2^{N_{\cal A}}}\sum_{g\in{\cal A}}\hat{D}_{g},\quad\hat{D}_{g}=\prod_{j\in g}\hat{D}_{j}. (28)

Using this factorization, we apply 𝒫D{\cal P}_{D} to Eq.(10) and obtain the explicit form of the Gutzwiller projected eigenstates of the original Hamiltonian, Eq.(11). By further expanding 𝒫D𝒜{\cal P}_{D}^{\cal A} and 𝒫Dℬ{\cal P}_{D}^{\cal B} in terms of D^i\hat{D}_{i}, we obtain the following form,

|Ψ𝒖,𝒗⟩\displaystyle|\Psi_{\bm{u},\bm{v}}\rangle =∑g∑{w𝒜},D𝒜=1∑ℓλℓ2N+L+1​Dg​|ψℓ𝒜⟩​|ψℓℬ⟩.\displaystyle=\sum_{g}\sum_{\{w_{\cal A}\},D_{\cal A}=1}\sum_{\ell}\frac{\lambda_{\ell}}{\sqrt{2^{N+L+1}}}D_{g}|\psi^{\cal A}_{\ell}\rangle|\psi^{\cal B}_{\ell}\rangle. (29)

B.2 How the Schmidt states are reduced by half.

Here, we explain the details of the derivation of Eq.(10) in the main text and related results. Let us divide the system into subsystems 𝒜{\cal A} and ℬ{\cal B} by drawing a closed loop as shown in Fig. 1(e) in the main text. Suppose that this closed loop cuts 2​L2L bonds on the lattice, which are indexed as 1,2,⋯,2n−1,2n,⋯2L1,2,\cdots,2n-1,2n,\cdots 2L, where we relabel the bond operator u^j\hat{u}_{j} as u^2​n−1\hat{u}_{2n-1} and u^2​n\hat{u}_{2n} labeled by α,β=x,y,z\alpha,\beta=x,y,z, and the corresponding fermionic operator b^ℛ,2​n−1α\hat{b}^{\alpha}_{{\cal R},2n-1} and b^ℛ,2​nβ\hat{b}^{\beta}_{{\cal R},2n} that belong to that bond on the 𝑹=𝒜,ℬ\bm{R}={\cal A,B} side. Next, we rearrange the bond operator on the nn-th hexagonal unit and define a set of states |w𝒜,n,wℬ,n⟩|w_{{\cal A},n},w_{{\cal B},n}\rangle as

f^1​n=12​(b^𝒜,2​n−1α+i​b^𝒜,2​nβ),f^2​n=12​(b^ℬ,2​n−1α+i​b^ℬ,2​nβ),\displaystyle\hat{f}_{1n}=\frac{1}{2}(\hat{b}_{{\cal A},2n-1}^{\alpha}+i\hat{b}_{{\cal A},2n}^{\beta}),\quad\hat{f}_{2n}=\frac{1}{2}(\hat{b}_{{\cal B},2n-1}^{\alpha}+i\hat{b}_{{\cal B},2n}^{\beta}),
𝒘n=|w𝒜,n,wℬ,n⟩={|1,−1⟩=f^†1​n|0⟩|−1,1⟩=−if^†2​n|0⟩|1,1⟩=f^†1​nf^†2​n|0⟩|−1,−1⟩=i|0⟩\displaystyle\bm{w}_{n}=|w_{{\cal A},n},w_{{\cal B},n}\rangle=\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}|1,-1\rangle=\hat{f}^{\dagger}_{1n}|0\rangle\\ |-1,1\rangle=-i\hat{f}^{\dagger}_{2n}|0\rangle\\ |1,1\rangle=\hat{f}^{\dagger}_{1n}\hat{f}^{\dagger}_{2n}|0\rangle\\ |-1,-1\rangle=i|0\rangle\\ \end{array}\right.

From this definition, the original gauge states 𝒖n=|u2​n−1,u2​n⟩=(|−1,−1⟩,|1,1⟩,|1,−1⟩,|−1,1⟩)T\bm{u}_{n}=|u_{2n-1},u_{2n}\rangle=(|-1,-1\rangle,|1,1\rangle,|1,-1\rangle,|-1,1\rangle)^{T} are related to 𝒘n\bm{w}_{n} as

𝒖n=12​(1−1111−111)​𝒘n.\displaystyle\bm{u}_{n}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left(\begin{array}[]{rrrr}1&-1\\ 1&1\\ &&1&-1\\ &&1&1\end{array}\right)\bm{w}_{n}.

Therefore, for a given 𝒖n\bm{u}_{n}, |w𝒜,n,wℬ,n⟩|w_{{\cal A},n},w_{{\cal B},n}\rangle has ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} degrees of freedom which we label wn=±1w_{n}=\pm 1; when u2​n−1=u2​nu_{2n-1}=u_{2n} it corresponds to the choice |1,−1⟩|1,-1\rangle and |−1,1⟩|-1,1\rangle, and when u2​n−1=−u2​nu_{2n-1}=-u_{2n}, |1,1⟩|1,1\rangle and |−1,−1⟩|-1,-1\rangle. Because a set of bond gauges 𝒖\bm{u} forms a product state, with this local gauge transformation around the loop, it can be separated into those inside region ℛ{\cal R} denoted as |𝒖ℛ⟩|\bm{u}^{\cal R}\rangle and those on the boundaries which are rearranged into |w𝒜,n,wℬ,n⟩|w_{{\cal A},n},w_{{\cal B},n}\rangle.

The separation of the bond-gauges into region 𝒜{\cal A} and ℬ{\cal B} so far discussed are based on Ref.[25] by Yao and Qi. In their framework, they applied the form Eq.(27) to describe the density matrix, ρ𝒜=TrB​(|Ψ𝒖,𝒏⟩​⟨Ψ𝒖,𝒏|)\rho_{\cal A}={\rm Tr}_{B}(|\Psi_{\bm{u},\bm{n}}\rangle\langle\Psi_{\bm{u},\bm{n}}|), where they operated D^g=X^g​𝒜​Y^g​𝒜​X^g​ℬ​Y^g​ℬ\hat{D}_{g}=\hat{X}_{g{\cal A}}\hat{Y}_{g{\cal A}}\hat{X}_{g{\cal B}}\hat{Y}_{g{\cal B}}, separately on the subsystems, each on bond gauge and matter parts. In this form (Eq.(A7) of the Supplemental [25]), the fermion parity in the matter state is constrained by the partial Gutzwiller projection Y^g​𝒜\hat{Y}_{g{\cal A}} and Y^g​ℬ\hat{Y}_{g{\cal B}}. Among the matter states, the ones that survive depend explicitly on the boundary gauge configuration, which then appears in their form of ρ𝒜\rho_{\cal A} as off-diagonal element of the projection operators, X^g​𝒜|u𝒜,w⟩⟨u𝒜,w|X^g​𝒜′†\hat{X}_{g{\cal A}}|u_{\cal A},w\rangle\langle u_{\cal A},w|\hat{X}_{g{\cal A}^{\prime}}^{\dagger}. In such a case, the Schmidt decomposition appears no longer to be carried out independently of the gauge sector, making the summation over gg and g′g^{\prime} (gauge transformation in Eq.(27) that appear inside ρ𝒜\rho_{\cal A}) highly nontrivial. Instead, Yao and Qi evaluated the integrated value Tr𝒜​[(ρ𝒜)n]{\rm Tr}_{\cal A}[(\rho_{\cal A})^{n}], applied the Replica trick, S=−∂∂n​Tr𝒜​[(ρ𝒜)n]|n=1S=-\frac{\partial}{\partial n}{\rm Tr}_{\cal A}[(\rho_{\cal A})^{n}]|_{n=1}, and obtained S=(L−1)​ln⁡2+α​LS=(L-1)\ln 2+\alpha L.

Our approach proceeds in the opposite order. Before applying the Gutzwiller projector, we first perform the exact Schmidt decomposition of the fermion wave function for both the matter and bond gauge parts (Eq.(10) in the main text),

|Ψ~𝒖,𝒗M⟩\displaystyle|\tilde{\Psi}^{M}_{\bm{u},\bm{v}}\rangle =|𝒖⟩|M𝒖⟩=(∑ℓ=1χλℓ|M𝒖​ℓA⟩|M𝒖​ℓB⟩)|𝒖A⟩|𝒖B⟩∑{wn=±1}∏n=1L|wA,n,wB,n⟩\displaystyle=|\bm{u}\rangle|M_{\bm{u}}\rangle=\Big(\sum_{\ell=1}^{\chi}\lambda_{\ell}|M^{A}_{\bm{u}\ell}\rangle|M^{B}_{\bm{u}\ell}\rangle\Big)|\bm{u}^{A}\rangle|\bm{u}^{B}\rangle\sum_{\{w_{n}=\pm 1\}}\prod_{n=1}^{L}|w_{A,n},w_{B,n}\rangle
=∑ℓ=1χ∑{wn=±1}(−)γλℓ2L(|M𝒖​ℓ𝒜⟩|𝒖𝒜⟩|w𝒜⟩)(|M𝒖​ℓℬ⟩|𝒖ℬ⟩|wℬ⟩),\displaystyle=\sum_{\ell=1}^{\chi}\sum_{\{w_{n}=\pm 1\}}(-)^{\gamma}\frac{\lambda_{\ell}}{\sqrt{2^{L}}}\Big(|M^{{\cal A}}_{\bm{u}\ell}\rangle|\bm{u}^{{\cal A}}\rangle|w^{{\cal A}}\rangle\Big)\Big(|M^{{\cal B}}_{\bm{u}\ell}\rangle|\bm{u}^{{\cal B}}\rangle|w^{{\cal B}}\rangle\Big), (38)

where the sign (−)γ(-)^{\gamma} comes from the combination of either of the two choices of |w𝒜,n,wℬ,n⟩|w_{{\cal A},n},w_{{\cal B},n}\rangle values in Eq.(B.2). The relevant summation ∑wn=±1\sum_{w_{n}=\pm 1} means that for each bond on a cut, there are two equivalent contributions from the choices of rearranged ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} bond gauges, that generate 2L2^{L} different terms. This contribution explains the highly degenerate Schmidt values found numerically in Fig. 2(d) in the main text.

Since a set of {uj}\{u_{j}\} are fixed values, the boundary gauges on the 2​L2L bonds should naturally satisfy ∏nw𝒜=η​∏nwℬ=±1\prod_{n}w_{\cal A}=\eta\prod_{n}w_{\cal B}=\pm 1 (where η\eta is either +1+1 or −1-1) under the D=1D=1 constraint. The two choices of the boundary gauge have one-to-one correspondence with the choice of D𝒜=±1D_{\cal A}=\pm 1.

In Eq.(38), Schmidt decomposing |M𝒖⟩|M_{\bm{u}}\rangle for a fixed bond gauge (classical variables) is trivial itself. However, as we clarify in the following equations, |M𝒖​ℓℛ⟩|M^{{\cal R}}_{\bm{u}\ell}\rangle are classified by the fermion parity in region ℛ=𝒜,ℬ{\cal R=A,B}, which has one-to-one correspondence with the boundary gauge sectors, which may not be trivial. This finding is a key to performing a full Schmidt decomposition of the physical state after the Gutzwiller projection (see Eq.(11)).

We now consider the global gauge operator, factorized into two parts, D^=D^𝒜⋅D^ℬ\hat{D}=\hat{D}_{\cal A}\cdot\hat{D}_{\cal B}, where D^ℛ=∏j∈ℛD^j\hat{D}_{\cal R}=\prod_{j\in{\cal R}}\hat{D}_{j}. The one operating on 𝒜{\cal A} can be expressed using a fermionic operator as

D^𝒜\displaystyle\hat{D}_{\cal A} =∏j∈𝒜D^j=∏j∈𝒜b^jx​b^jy​b^jz​c^j\displaystyle=\prod_{j\in{\cal A}}\hat{D}_{j}=\prod_{j\in{\cal A}}\hat{b}_{j}^{x}\hat{b}_{j}^{y}\hat{b}_{j}^{z}\hat{c}_{j}
=(−)m​∏ui​j∈𝒜u^i​j​∏n=1Lw^𝒜,n​∏l∈𝒜c^l,\displaystyle=(-)^{m}\prod_{u_{ij}\in{\cal A}}\hat{u}_{ij}\prod_{n=1}^{L}\hat{w}_{{\cal A},n}\prod_{l\in{\cal A}}\hat{c}_{l}, (39)

with the sign (−)m(-)^{m} properly chosen. Since the matter Schmidt states, |M𝒖​ℓℛ⟩|M^{\cal R}_{\bm{u}\ell}\rangle, on region 𝒜{\cal A} and ℬ{\cal B} are both free Majorana states, they are the eigenstates of ∏l∈ℛc^l\prod_{l\in{\cal R}}\hat{c}_{l} with eigenvalues ±1\pm 1; the operator QQ that transforms Majorana to fermions has ∏ℓcℓ=det⁡(Q)​∏ℓ(1−2​nℓ′)\prod_{\ell}c_{\ell}={\rm det}(Q)\prod_{\ell}(1-2n^{\prime}_{\ell}) with nℓ′n^{\prime}_{\ell} the fermion number operator (see Ref.[39] Appendix A for details). Therefore, one can straightforwardly show that,

D^𝒜​|M𝒖​ℓ𝒜⟩​|𝒖𝒜⟩​|w𝒜⟩=±|M𝒖​ℓ𝒜⟩​|𝒖𝒜⟩​|w𝒜⟩,\hat{D}_{\cal A}|M^{{\cal A}}_{\bm{u}\ell}\rangle|\bm{u}^{{\cal A}}\rangle|w^{{\cal A}}\rangle=\pm|M^{{\cal A}}_{\bm{u}\ell}\rangle|\bm{u}^{{\cal A}}\rangle|w^{{\cal A}}\rangle, (40)

where ±1\pm 1 eigenvalues come from the two choices of boundary gauge states |w𝒜⟩|w^{\cal A}\rangle, as |u𝒜⟩|u^{\cal A}\rangle is unique about u^i​j\hat{u}_{ij}.

With these informations, one can say that |Ψ~𝒖,𝒗M⟩|\tilde{\Psi}^{M}_{\bm{u},\bm{v}}\rangle is the D=1D=1 eigenstate and its Schmidt state {|ψℓ𝒜⟩}\{|\psi^{\cal A}_{\ell}\rangle\} includes two eigenstates of D𝒜=±1D_{\cal A}=\pm 1. However, since 𝒫D{\cal P}_{D} enforces D𝒜=1D_{\cal A}=1, only half of them remain, which explains that the number of Schmidt states is reduced by half for each λℓ\lambda_{\ell} and accordingly, λℓ\lambda_{\ell} is scaled by 2\sqrt{2}. Using Eq.(40), one can separately operate the Gutzwiller projection to 𝒜{\cal A} and ℬ{\cal B} parts of the Schmidt form in |Ψ~𝒖,𝒗M⟩|\tilde{\Psi}^{M}_{\bm{u},\bm{v}}\rangle, and |Ψ𝒖,𝒗⟩|\Psi_{\bm{u},\bm{v}}\rangle of the spin Hamiltonian is also Schmidt decomposed as in Eq.(11) of Sec. III.3.

Appendix C Spatial range that the Majorana fermion occupies

We want to obtain a quantum number of subsystem 𝒜\cal A that characterizes this subspace. The value of {𝒖}∈𝒜\{\bm{u}\}\in{\cal A} is local and trivial, whereas aℓ/aℓ†a_{\ell}/a_{\ell}^{\dagger} acts on all the sites, so that the number of localized Majorana fermions needs to be calculated.

Suppose the free Majorana state before projection, |Ψ~rM⟩≡|Ψ~u,nM⟩|\tilde{\Psi}^{M}_{r}\rangle\equiv|\tilde{\Psi}^{M}_{u,n}\rangle, has an ℓ\ell th Majorana, nℓ=1n_{\ell}=1 (or not, nℓ=0n_{\ell}=0), which is read off as a^ℓ†​|Ψ~rM⟩=0\hat{a}_{\ell}^{\dagger}|\tilde{\Psi}^{M}_{r}\rangle=0 (or a^ℓ​|Ψ~rM⟩=0\hat{a}_{\ell}|\tilde{\Psi}^{M}_{r}\rangle=0). For a given set of values, {nℓ}ℓ=1N/2\{n_{\ell}\}_{\ell=1}^{N/2}, one can define a vector 𝒂^={a^l×}l=1⋯,N/2\hat{\bm{a}}=\{\hat{a}_{l}^{\times}\}_{l=1\cdots,N/2}, where ×=†\times={\dagger} for nl=1n_{l}=1 and ×\times means nothing otherwise. Then, the condition that the state needs to satisfy to have these Majorana numbers is given as a set of linear equations, 𝒂^​|Ψ~rM⟩=𝟎\hat{\bm{a}}|\tilde{\Psi}^{M}_{r}\rangle=\bm{0}. By substituting a^ℓ=1/2∑j=1NQj​ℓcj\hat{a}_{\ell}=1/\sqrt{2}\sum_{j=1}^{N}Q_{j\ell}c_{j} with 𝒄={cj}j=1⋯,N\bm{c}=\{c_{j}\}_{j=1\cdots,N}, we find

Q~​𝒄​|Ψ~rM⟩=0,\displaystyle\tilde{Q}\bm{c}|\tilde{\Psi}^{M}_{r}\rangle=0, (41)

where the Q~={Q~ℓ​j}\tilde{Q}=\{\tilde{Q}_{\ell j}\} is the N/2×NN/2\times N matrix that satisfies Q~ℓ​j=Qj​ℓ∗\tilde{Q}_{\ell j}=Q^{\ast}_{j\ell} (or Qj​ℓQ_{j\ell}) for nℓ=1n_{\ell}=1 (or 0). This matrix is rewritten as

Q~=U​L,\displaystyle\tilde{Q}=UL, (42)

using the unitary matrix UU and lower triangular matrix LL. One then finds that a new set of Majorana fermions, 𝒂^′={a^l′}l=1⋯,N/2\hat{\bm{a}}^{\prime}=\{\hat{a}_{l}^{\prime}\}_{l=1\cdots,N/2}, transformed from 𝒂^=U​𝒂^′\hat{\bm{a}}=U\hat{\bm{a}}^{\prime}, and because of the lower triangular form of LL, 𝒂′\bm{a}^{\prime} acts only on the subsystem ranging within [1:N/2+ℓ][1:N/2+\ell]. It means that one can specify which Majorana, ℓ\ell, is localized in region 𝒜{\cal A} (1:k1:k) by judging that if k≥N/2+ℓk\geq N/2+\ell, it satisfies a^l′⁣†​a^l′=0\hat{a}_{l}^{\prime{\dagger}}\hat{a}_{l}^{\prime}=0, and otherwise nonlocalized. We could list the localized Majoranas and fully characterize 𝒱k,r𝒜{\cal V}_{k,r}^{\cal A} accordingly. One important conclusion here is that all the Majoranas are spread over more than half the system size, regardless of the shape or size of the cluster.

Appendix D Details of Parton theory

D.1 Schmidt decomposition

We first Fourier transform Eq.(16) as, f𝒌​s​σ=Nc−1/2∑l=1Ncei​𝒌​𝒓l,sfl​s​σf_{\bm{k}s\sigma}=N_{c}^{-1/2}\sum_{l=1}^{N_{c}}e^{i\bm{k}\bm{r}_{l,s}}f_{ls\sigma} where we redefined fl​s​σf_{ls\sigma} as the Abrikosov fermion in the l(=1,⋯,Nc)l(=1,\cdots,N_{c}) th unit cell on s(=1,⋯,ns)s(=1,\cdots,n_{s}) th site (j∈(l,s)j\in(l,s)). For the kagome lattice, Nc=N/6N_{c}=N/6 and ns=6n_{s}=6, shown in Fig. 8(a). The Hamiltonian is transformed as

ℋp=\displaystyle{\cal H}_{p}= ∑𝒌,σ∑s,s′f𝒌​s​σ†​Ws,s′​(𝒌)​f𝒌​s′​σ\displaystyle\sum_{\bm{k},\sigma}\sum_{s,s^{\prime}}f_{\bm{k}s\sigma}^{\dagger}W_{s,s^{\prime}}(\bm{k})f_{\bm{k}s^{\prime}\sigma}
+∑𝒌∑s,s′(f𝒌​s↑†Ds,s′(𝒌)f−𝒌​s′↓†+h.c.).\displaystyle\quad+\sum_{\bm{k}}\sum_{s,s^{\prime}}(f^{\dagger}_{\bm{k}s\uparrow}D_{s,s^{\prime}}(\bm{k})f^{\dagger}_{-\bm{k}s^{\prime}\downarrow}+h.c.). (43)

When Δi​j=ζ=0\Delta_{ij}=\zeta=0, we find Ds,s′=0D_{s,s^{\prime}}=0 so that we only need to diagonalize the ns×nsn_{s}\times n_{s} matrix WW with Qσ,σ=↑,↓Q^{\sigma},\sigma=\uparrow,\downarrow, as Qσ†WQσ=diag(ϵℓ(𝒌))ℓ=1,⋯nsQ^{\sigma^{\dagger}}WQ^{\sigma}={\rm diag}(\epsilon_{\ell}(\bm{k}))_{\ell=1,\cdots n_{s}}, with the corresponding fermions given as, f~𝒌​ℓ​σ=∑sQℓ​sσ†f𝒌​s​σ\tilde{f}_{\bm{k}\ell\sigma}=\sum_{s}Q_{\ell s}^{\sigma\dagger}f_{\bm{k}s\sigma}.

Whereas when Δi​j≠0\Delta_{ij}\neq 0, the Hamiltonian has a Bogoliubov-de-Gennes form,

ℋp\displaystyle{\cal H}_{p} =∑𝒌>0𝚿𝒌†​H​(𝒌)​𝚿𝒌,\displaystyle=\sum_{\bm{k}>0}\bm{\Psi}_{\bm{k}}^{\dagger}H(\bm{k})\bm{\Psi}_{\bm{k}},
H⁡(𝒌)=(W⁡(𝒌)D⁡(𝒌)Dt∗(𝒌)−W⁡(𝒌)),\displaystyle H(\bm{k})=\left(\begin{array}[]{rr}W(\bm{k})&D(\bm{k})\\ D^{t*}(\bm{k})&-W(\bm{k})\end{array}\right),
𝚿𝒌†=(f𝒌,1,↑†,⋯,f𝒌,ns,↑†,⋯,f−𝒌,1,↓,⋯,f−𝒌,ns,↓),\displaystyle\bm{\Psi}_{\bm{k}}^{\dagger}=(f^{\dagger}_{\bm{k},1,\uparrow},\cdots,f^{\dagger}_{\bm{k},n_{s},\uparrow},\cdots,f_{-\bm{k},1,\downarrow},\cdots,f_{-\bm{k},n_{s},\downarrow}), (46)

and by diagonalizing the 2​ns×2​ns2n_{s}\times 2n_{s} matrix HH as Q†​H​Q=diag​({−w𝒌,ℓ},{w𝒌,ℓ})ℓ=1,⋯,nsQ^{\dagger}HQ={\rm diag}(\{-w_{\bm{k},\ell}\},\{w_{\bm{k},\ell}\})_{\ell=1,\cdots,n_{s}}, we obtain a Bogoliubov fermion (b𝒌,ℓ,b−𝒌​ℓ†)=Q†​Ψ𝒌(b_{\bm{k},\ell},b_{-\bm{k}\ell}^{\dagger})=Q^{\dagger}\Psi_{\bm{k}}, and the corresponding superconducting energy band ±w𝒌,ℓ\pm w_{\bm{k},\ell}. Here, we set the chemical potential to have the system half-filled, which is inside the band gap.

We now prepare a correlation matrix CC for the Majorana fermions in Eq.(17), {cl​s​σ;α}\{c_{ls\sigma;\alpha}\} with (α=1,2\alpha=1,2) as

C(l​s​σ,α,l′​s′​σ′,α′)=⟨cl​s​σ;α​cl′​s′​σ′;α′⟩,\displaystyle C_{(ls\sigma;\alpha,l^{\prime}s^{\prime}\sigma^{\prime};\alpha^{\prime})}=\langle c_{ls\sigma;\alpha}c_{l^{\prime}s^{\prime}\sigma^{\prime};\alpha^{\prime}}\rangle, (47)
⟨cl​s​σ;1​cl′​s′​σ′;1⟩=⟨fl​s​σ†​fl′​s′​σ′+fl​s​σ​fl′​s′​σ′†+fl​s​σ†​fl′​s′​σ′†+fl​s​σ​fl′​s′​σ′⟩,\displaystyle\quad\quad\langle c_{ls\sigma;1}c_{l^{\prime}s^{\prime}\sigma^{\prime};1}\rangle=\langle f_{ls\sigma}^{\dagger}f_{l^{\prime}s^{\prime}\sigma^{\prime}}+f_{ls\sigma}f_{l^{\prime}s^{\prime}\sigma^{\prime}}^{\dagger}+f_{ls\sigma}^{\dagger}f_{l^{\prime}s^{\prime}\sigma^{\prime}}^{\dagger}+f_{ls\sigma}f_{l^{\prime}s^{\prime}\sigma^{\prime}}\rangle,
⟨cl​s​σ;2​cl′​s′​σ′;2⟩=⟨fl​s​σ†​fl′​s′​σ′+fl​s​σ​fl′​s′​σ′†−fl​s​σ†​fl′​s′​σ′†−fl​s​σ​fl′​s′​σ′⟩,\displaystyle\quad\quad\langle c_{ls\sigma;2}c_{l^{\prime}s^{\prime}\sigma^{\prime};2}\rangle=\langle f_{ls\sigma}^{\dagger}f_{l^{\prime}s^{\prime}\sigma^{\prime}}+f_{ls\sigma}f_{l^{\prime}s^{\prime}\sigma^{\prime}}^{\dagger}-f_{ls\sigma}^{\dagger}f_{l^{\prime}s^{\prime}\sigma^{\prime}}^{\dagger}-f_{ls\sigma}f_{l^{\prime}s^{\prime}\sigma^{\prime}}\rangle,
⟨cl​s​σ;1​cl′​s′​σ′;2⟩=(−i)​⟨fl​s​σ†​fl′​s′​σ′−fl​s​σ​fl′​s′​σ′†−fl​s​σ†​fl′​s′​σ′†+fl​s​σ​fl′​s′​σ′⟩\displaystyle\quad\quad\langle c_{ls\sigma;1}c_{l^{\prime}s^{\prime}\sigma^{\prime};2}\rangle=(-i)\langle f_{ls\sigma}^{\dagger}f_{l^{\prime}s^{\prime}\sigma^{\prime}}-f_{ls\sigma}f_{l^{\prime}s^{\prime}\sigma^{\prime}}^{\dagger}-f_{ls\sigma}^{\dagger}f_{l^{\prime}s^{\prime}\sigma^{\prime}}^{\dagger}+f_{ls\sigma}f_{l^{\prime}s^{\prime}\sigma^{\prime}}\rangle
⟨cl​s​σ;2​cl′​s′​σ′;1⟩=i⁡⟨fl​s​σ†​fl′​s′​σ′−fl​s​σ​fl′​s′​σ′†+fl​s​σ†​fl′​s′​σ′†−fl​s​σ​fl′​s′​σ′⟩,\displaystyle\quad\quad\langle c_{ls\sigma;2}c_{l^{\prime}s^{\prime}\sigma^{\prime};1}\rangle=i\langle f_{ls\sigma}^{\dagger}f_{l^{\prime}s^{\prime}\sigma^{\prime}}-f_{ls\sigma}f_{l^{\prime}s^{\prime}\sigma^{\prime}}^{\dagger}+f_{ls\sigma}^{\dagger}f_{l^{\prime}s^{\prime}\sigma^{\prime}}^{\dagger}-f_{ls\sigma}f_{l^{\prime}s^{\prime}\sigma^{\prime}}\rangle, (48)

where ⟨fl​s​σ†​fl′​s′​σ′⟩\langle f_{ls\sigma}^{\dagger}f_{l^{\prime}s^{\prime}\sigma^{\prime}}\rangle is obtained by transforming its representation to Bogoliubov fermions.

When dividing the system into subsystems 𝒜{\cal A} and ℬ{\cal B}, the Schmidt values are given as a submatrix of CC, whose column and row indices belong to region A: C𝒜=C(m,m′)∈𝒜≡δm​m′+i​(Γ𝒜)m​m′C_{\cal A}=C_{(m,m^{\prime})\in{\cal A}}\equiv\delta_{mm^{\prime}}+i(\Gamma_{\cal A})_{mm^{\prime}}, with m=(l​s​σ​α)m=(ls\sigma\alpha) Diagonalizing C𝒜−1=i​Γ𝒜C_{\cal A}-1=i\Gamma_{\cal A}, we obtain a set of 2​N𝒜2N_{\cal A} pairs of eigenvalues as

Q𝒜†​(i​Γ)​Q𝒜=diag​({±νm})m=12​N𝒜,0≤νm≤1,\displaystyle Q_{\cal A}^{\dagger}(i\Gamma)Q_{\cal A}={\rm diag}\big(\,\{\pm\nu_{m}\}\,\big)_{m=1}^{2N_{\cal A}},\quad 0\leq\nu_{m}\leq 1,
(c~1,⋯,c~2​m−1,c~2​m,⋯,c~2​N𝒜)\displaystyle(\tilde{c}_{1},\cdots,\tilde{c}_{2m-1},\tilde{c}_{2m},\cdots,\tilde{c}_{2N_{\cal A}})
=\displaystyle= Q𝒜(c1,⋯,c2​m−1,c2​m,⋯c2​N𝒜).\displaystyle Q_{\cal A}(c_{1},\cdots,c_{2m-1},c_{2m},\cdots c_{2N_{\cal A}}). (49)

They are put back to the fermionic operator in region 𝒜{\cal A} as b~m=(c~2​m−1+i​c~2​m)/2\tilde{b}_{m}=(\tilde{c}_{2m-1}+i\tilde{c}_{2m})/2, and its number is described by the eigenvalues as ⟨b~m†​b~m⟩=(1+νm)/2\langle\tilde{b}_{m}^{\dagger}\tilde{b}_{m}\rangle=(1+\nu_{m})/2. Following Ref.[52], the Schmidt value is obtained for each set ℓ≡{nm𝒜}m=12​N𝒜\ell\equiv\{n_{m}^{\cal A}\}_{m=1}^{2N_{\cal A}} as

λℓ=∏m=12​N𝒜1+(−)nm𝒜​νm2.\displaystyle\lambda_{\ell}=\prod_{m=1}^{2N_{\cal A}}\frac{1+(-)^{n_{m}^{\cal A}}\nu_{m}}{2}. (50)

The important notice is that each Schmidt state |ψℓ𝒜⟩|\psi_{\ell}^{\cal A}\rangle labeled by ℓ=1,⋯,2​N𝒜\ell=1,\cdots,2N_{\cal A}, is the eigenstate of D^𝒜\hat{D}_{\cal A} because,

D^𝒜\displaystyle\hat{D}_{\cal A} =∏(ℓ,s)∈𝒜cℓ​s↑;1​cℓ​s↑;2​cℓ​s↓;1​cℓ​s↓;2\displaystyle=\prod_{(\ell,s)\in{\cal A}}c_{\ell s\uparrow;1}c_{\ell s\uparrow;2}c_{\ell s\downarrow;1}c_{\ell s\downarrow;2}
→D𝒜=det​Q𝒜​∏m=12​N𝒜(−1)nm𝒜.\displaystyle\quad\rightarrow\;\;D_{\cal A}={\rm det}Q_{\cal A}\prod_{m=1}^{2N_{\cal A}}(-1)^{n_{m}^{\cal A}}. (51)

This allows us to evaluate D𝒜D_{\cal A} for each Schmidt state.

When the U(1) symmetry is kept, the correlation matrix is block diagonalized into up and down spin sectors, and thus the Schmidt values become the product of the two spin sectors as

λℓ=∏m=1N𝒜1+(−)nm↑​νm2​∏m′=1N𝒜1+(−)nm′↓​νm′2.\displaystyle\lambda_{\ell}=\prod_{m=1}^{N_{\cal A}}\frac{1+(-)^{n_{m\uparrow}}\nu_{m}}{2}\prod_{m^{\prime}=1}^{N_{\cal A}}\frac{1+(-)^{n_{m^{\prime}\downarrow}}\nu_{m^{\prime}}}{2}. (52)

This fact indicates that the Schmidt states are completely separable between the up and down spin components, namely, the two components have zero entanglement. In that case, the entanglement entropy is determined (as in the case of standard free fermions) by counting the probability of each one-body fermionic eigenstate having the distributions on both sides. When the U(1) symmetry is broken and the gap opens, the ℤ2{\mathbb{Z}}_{2} spin liquid state is obtained. This state is analogous to the superconductivity of the Kitaev chain, in which case the fermions form a Cooper pair. Their entanglement entropy is obtained by counting the probability distribution of each Cooper-pair eigenstate, which number is roughly half the original fermionic number (see Fig. 7(b)). This explains why the introduction of Δ2≠0\Delta_{2}\neq 0 reduces the entanglement entropy by half from the U(1) case in Fig. 4(a) in the main text (see also Fig.7(a)).

D.2 Pfaffian and U(1) and ℤ2{\mathbb{Z}}_{2} Spin liquids

In this subsection, we explain in detail how the definition of DD in Eq.(12) in the main text is related to the characterization of the spin liquid. In the same way as Eq.(12) in the main text, the global operator D^\hat{D} is given in the form,

D^\displaystyle\hat{D} =∏(ℓ,s)cℓ​s↑;1​cl​s↑;2​cℓ​s↓;1​cℓ​s↓;2\displaystyle=\prod_{(\ell,s)}c_{\ell s\uparrow;1}c_{ls\uparrow;2}c_{\ell s\downarrow;1}c_{\ell s\downarrow;2}
→D=det​Q​∏m=12​N(−1)nm=sgn⁡(Pf⁡(A))​(−)∑mnm,\displaystyle\quad\rightarrow\;\;D={\rm det}Q\prod_{m=1}^{2N}(-1)^{n_{m}}={\rm sgn}({\rm Pf}(A))(-)^{\sum_{m}n_{m}}, (53)

where nm=0,1n_{m}=0,1 is the number of fermions occupying the mm-th eigenstate of Eq.(46), AA is an antisymmetrc matrix defined as ℋp=i4​∑ℓ​s​σ;α,ℓ′​s′​σ′;α′Aℓ​s​σ;α,ℓ′​s′​σ′;α′​cℓ​s​σ;α​cℓ′​s′​σ′;α′{\cal H}_{p}=\frac{i}{4}\sum_{\ell s\sigma;\alpha,\;\ell^{\prime}s^{\prime}\sigma^{\prime};\alpha^{\prime}}A_{\ell s\sigma;\alpha,\;\ell^{\prime}s^{\prime}\sigma^{\prime};\alpha^{\prime}}c_{\ell s\sigma;\alpha}c_{\ell^{\prime}s^{\prime}\sigma^{\prime};\alpha^{\prime}} and det​Q=(−)2​N​det​A/Pf⁡(A)=sgn⁡(Pf⁡(A)){\rm det}Q=(-)^{2N}\sqrt{{\rm det}A}/{\rm Pf}(A)={\rm sgn}({\rm Pf}(A)).

Let us make some remarks on the relationship between DD and the Pfaffian. When Δi​j=ζi​j=0\Delta_{ij}=\zeta_{ij}=0 with unbroken U(1) symmetry, the up and down-spin fermions are decoupled, so that Q↑=Q↓Q^{\uparrow}=Q^{\downarrow}. The Bogoliubov fermion number for spin σ\sigma is defined as nm​σn_{m\sigma}, with nm=nm↑+nm↓n_{m}=n_{m\uparrow}+n_{m\downarrow}. Then, DD reduces to

D=det​Q↑​det​Q↓​∏m=1N(−1)nm↑+nm↓=∏m=1N(−1)nm↑+nm↓,\displaystyle D={\rm det}Q^{\uparrow}{\rm det}Q^{\downarrow}\prod_{m=1}^{N}(-1)^{n_{m\uparrow}+n_{m\downarrow}}=\prod_{m=1}^{N}(-1)^{n_{m\uparrow}+n_{m\downarrow}}, (54)

which means that DD no longer depends on the Pfaffian, as we always find det​Q=det​Q↑​det​Q↓=(det​Q↓)2=1{\rm det}Q={\rm det}Q^{\uparrow}{\rm det}Q^{\downarrow}=({\rm det}Q^{\downarrow})^{2}=1.

The characterization of the U(1) spin liquid is given by Wen[53] using a Wilson loop operator along the closed loop CC ; Using a matrix Ui​jU_{ij} defined on an ⟨i​j⟩\langle ij\rangle neighboring bond, the matrix representation of the Wilson loop is given as

Ui​j=(χi​jΔi​jΔi​j∗−χi​j),𝒫C=∏⟨i,j⟩∈CUi​j.U_{ij}=\left(\begin{array}[]{rr}\chi_{ij}&\Delta_{ij}\\ \Delta_{ij}^{*}&-\chi_{ij}\end{array}\right),\quad\quad{\cal P}_{C}=\prod_{\langle i,j\rangle\in C}U_{ij}. (55)

When Δi​j=0\Delta_{ij}=0, Ui​jU_{ij} is diagonal and accordingly, Wilson loop commutes, [PC,PC′]=0[P_{C},P_{C^{\prime}}]=0. In this case, χi​j≠0\chi_{ij}\neq 0 yields a U(1) spin liquid.

When Δi​j≠0\Delta_{ij}\neq 0, the noncommutative loops, [PC,PC′]≠0[P_{C},P_{C^{\prime}}]\neq 0, yield a ℤ2{\mathbb{Z}}_{2} spin liquid. This means that from Eq.(53), we can find det​Q≠1{\rm det}Q\neq 1 only when the U(1) symmetry is broken, in which case sgn⁡(Pf⁡(A)){\rm sgn(Pf}(A)) enters DD.

D.3 Numerical results

We now demonstrate the validity of applying parton theory to the S=1/2S=1/2 kagome and triangular lattice J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} Heisenberg models. For the kagome lattice, we adopted χi​j=±χ1\chi_{ij}=\pm\chi_{1} for the nearest neighbor bonds and χi​j=±χ2\chi_{ij}=\pm\chi_{2} for the next-nearest neighbor bonds in a configuration shown in Fig. 8(a) with six-site unit cell. The plus and minus bonds are shown in solid and broken lines, respectively, corresponding to the ℤ2​[0,π]​β{\mathbb{Z}}_{2}[0,\pi]\beta ansatz. The parameter values are taken from the variational Monte Carlo study (VMC) in Ref.[48] as (χ1,χ2)=(1,−0.0186)(\chi_{1},\chi_{2})=(1,-0.0186). For a U(1) spin liquid, Δ2=ζ=0\Delta_{2}=\zeta=0, and for the ℤ2{\mathbb{Z}}_{2} spin liquid, we choose Δ2,ζ≠0\Delta_{2},\zeta\neq 0 by hand. In the VMC studies [48, 54], the optimization of parameters reach Δ2=ζ=0\Delta_{2}=\zeta=0, while their convergence is not as good as the energy itself; the free energy landscape about Δ2\Delta_{2}, that connects U(1) and ℤ2​[0,π]​β{\mathbb{Z}}_{2}[0,\pi]\beta, is reported to be very flat. This indicates the actual difficulty of determining which is stable, solely by numerical simulations, as has been discussed for decades[55]. Here, we do not aim to discuss this issue, but instead, make direct comparison of the entanglement property between the parton spin liquid state and the ℤ2{\mathbb{Z}}_{2} spin liquid reported previously in the DMRG study[47].

We first show the results of the kagome lattice calculated on a series of YC cylinders shown in the inset of Fig. 7; the periodic boundary (PBC) taken in the yy-direction, and its circumference is c=2​Nyc=2N_{y}, where we set Nx=32N_{x}=32 and Ny=4−10N_{y}=4-10, with N=6​Nx​NyN=6N_{x}N_{y} up to 1920 sites. We show in Fig. 7(a), the Rényi-α\alpha entropy defined as

Sαf=11−α​ln⁡(Tr)A​[(ρA)α],\displaystyle S_{\alpha}^{f}=\frac{1}{1-\alpha}\ln{\rm Tr}_{A}[(\rho_{A})^{\alpha}], (56)

to compare with those obtained by the cylinder DMRG in Ref.[47]. We plot α=2,3,4,5\alpha=2,3,4,5 for the U(1) parton state, where α=2\alpha=2 data is the same as the one plotted in Fig. 4(a) in the main text. As we show in the inset for the c=20c=20 case, breaking the U(1) symmetry down to ℤ2{\mathbb{Z}}_{2} by the introduction of Δ2≠0\Delta_{2}\neq 0 reduces SαS_{\alpha} by half. Then, we find that the slope of Sα/2S_{\alpha}/2 of our Parton Hamiltonian (fermions) for all α\alpha in the main panel is comparable to the one obtained by DMRG in the S=1/2S=1/2 kagome Heisenberg antiferromagnet (see Fig. 6 of Ref.[47]). The difference is the emergent −ln⁡2-\ln 2; it means that the D𝒜=1D_{\cal A}=1 sector of the parton state has quantitatively the same entanglement scaling law as the spin liquid state in DMRG, and that the Gutzwiller projection is the origin of the −ln⁡2-\ln 2 term.

To examine how the two D𝒜D_{\cal A} sectors emerge, we plot in Fig. 7(b) the distribution of the eigenvalues of the correlation matrix, νm\nu_{m}, which generates λℓ\lambda_{\ell} according to Eq.(50). Here, naively, νm\nu_{m} is considered as an occupation number of fermionic particles. By comparing the case of Δ2=ζ=0\Delta_{2}=\zeta=0 (U(1)) and 0.30.3 (ℤ2{\mathbb{Z}}_{2}), the occupation is roughly reduced by half, which is intuitively understood as the aforementioned analogy with the Kitaev superconductor, that the pairing of fermions reduces the occupation number by half. In fact, as we showed in the main text, introducing Δ2=ζ≠0\Delta_{2}=\zeta\neq 0 will almost perfectly support the half-reduction of the entanglement entropy due to the breaking of U(1) symmetry. We then further show in Fig. 7(c) the Schmidt values, λℓ\lambda_{\ell}, for the U(1) and ℤ2{\mathbb{Z}}_{2} states. The Schmidt spectrum splits into two nearly degenerate D𝒜=±1D_{\cal A}=\pm 1 sectors, and by definition, the Gutzwiller projection removes the −1-1 sector to put the state back to the spin representation, where the −ln⁡2-\ln 2 appears.

Figure 8(c) shows the results of the parton theory for the same kagome lattice antiferromagnet on a torus (PBC in two different directions shown in the inset), where the unit cell is the shaded nc=6n_{c}=6 sites. We calculated the Schmidt values for subsystem 𝒜{\cal A} consisting of N𝒜=12N_{\cal A}=12 sites shown in the panel; they are separated into almost equivalent D𝒜=±1D_{\cal A}=\pm 1 sectors, where the finite-size (shape) effects are less pronounced than in the cylinders. The excited state has the same feature with more precise degeneracies. The size scaling of the entanglement entropy as a function of N𝒜​x=N𝒜​yN_{{\cal A}x}=N_{{\cal A}y} is shown in the inset, which linearly extrapolates to zero. By removing the D𝒜=−1D_{\cal A}=-1 contribution from it, we obtain the −ln⁡2-\ln 2 term.

We also performed the same calculation for the triangular lattice J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} antiferromagnet [56] shown in Fig. 8(b), where we set the nearest neighbor χi​j=±1\chi_{ij}=\pm 1 as solid and broken lines with ns=4n_{s}=4 site unit cell, which has a π\pi flux on the upward triangle. By setting Nx=Ny=10N_{x}=N_{y}=10 with N=4​Nx​Ny=400N=4N_{x}N_{y}=400, and the subsystem 𝒜{\cal A} as N𝒜=12N_{\cal A}=12 shown in Fig. 8(d), we find results similar to the kagome lattice case. The size scaling for Nx𝒜=Ny𝒜N_{x}^{\cal A}=N_{y}^{\cal A} shows a linear slope toward zero, which we can expect to acquire −ln⁡2-\ln 2 after Gutzwiller projection onto the D𝒜=1D_{\cal A}=1 sector. Unfortunately, unlike the kagome lattice, there are no rigorous numerical simulations that exhibit the entanglement entropy (or Rényi entropy) scaling, which makes the direct comparison difficult. However, the features observed here for the parton Hamiltonian are basically equivalent to the kagome lattice. This fact strongly supports the general picture of the reduction of Schmidt states as the cause of the topological term.
